articles.title: ‘Aether & Iron’: Seattle-area indie game studio builds a noir detective RPG in the sky
articles.author: Thomas Wilde
paras: Some video games exist at the confluence point between a surprising number of genres, which can make them difficult to explain to people who aren’t hip-deep in the hobby. That’s why several of the most popular categories are currently nicknamed after the most visible games in them, such as the “ Metroidvania ” or “ Soulslike .” Sure, this isn’t anywhere near the biggest problem in the video game industry at the moment, but we’re going to have to figure this out sooner or later.

Aether & Iron, created by the Issaquah, Wash.-based developer Seismic Squirrel , with co-developer Chaos Theory Games, is at one of those weird genre points. It’s described by its developers as a “narrative RPG,” which works well enough, but that also doesn’t exactly say that much.

It’s worth saying up front that Aether & Iron is on a slow boil. It’s a 30-hour game that unfolds at a careful pace, building out an elaborate science-fiction setting from first principles. If you’re looking for fast thrills, it’s not the experience for you. Instead, think of it like a long novel with points of potential failure, where every opportunity for interactivity is also a chance for you to take its story in a different direction.

Aether & Iron is set in an alternate universe where a strange substance called aether was found beneath Manhattan in 1871. Sixty-seven years later, the study and exploitation of aether has become its own branch of science, which led to a great technological leap forward. Much of New York has been transformed into a three-tiered flying city, split between the Lowers, the Uppers and the Heights. The higher a neighborhood flies, the higher its society.

You enter the story in 1938 in the role of Gia Randazzo, a smuggler from the Lowers who’s hit hard times. She’s so desperate for work that she takes a job she shouldn’t, as a driver and bodyguard for a young scientist from the Heights named Eleanor Reinhardt. It should be a milk run, but Dr. Reinhardt has enemies she doesn’t know about.

In short order, an assassin tries to kill them both, someone steals Gia’s car, and she and Dr. Reinhardt end up stuck together in the worst parts of the Lowers. With no money, a loaner vehicle and few friends left, Gia has to figure out who wants Dr. Reinhardt dead and why. That puts her on a collision course with a revolutionary movement, several of New York’s power brokers and a conspiracy that could knock the city back out of the sky.

You could call Aether & Iron something like “airship noir.” Despite its science-fiction trappings, it’s a dark detective novel at heart. Yes, humanity’s built up into the sky, but the street is always the street. Mickey Spillane meets William Gibson.

During dialogue and investigation sequences, Aether & Iron uses a pair of virtual six-sided dice to determine whether you succeed or fail at a given task. As you get further into the game, you can acquire items that let you reroll those dice on a failed check.

More importantly, you earn experience points for accomplishments and victories, which grant you skill points that can be spent in one of nine categories. You can customize Gia to follow several distinct character tracks, such as a detective, a back-alley brawler or a fast-talking con woman. That influences the path you take through the game and the options that become available to you.

No matter how you choose to play Gia, you can’t always avoid a fight. All the combat in Aether & Iron takes place behind the wheel, with Gia and her crew driving customized vehicles. You can acquire a whole fleet of cars and trucks, then kit them out with special weapons, utility devices, armored plates and matching paint jobs.

Each fight consists of a turn-based tactical battle through the streets in and around New York. In addition to simply shooting up an enemy, you can sideswipe them to force them off the road or into other cars.

Many of the city’s thoroughfares are falling apart or prone to sudden lane changes, so most fights will have their own set of additional hazards. Fortunately, they’re as dangerous to your enemies as they are to you, so you can exploit the road hazards if you think fast enough.

If I had to point at one problem I’ve got with Aether & Iron, it might be that the combat has a couple of unlabeled difficulty curves. Specifically, a few fights are built around specific types of damage to such a degree that the only real way past them is to reload an old save and modify all my vehicles for that particular encounter.

If you like the idea of constantly tweaking your vehicle collection for specific combat purposes, like heat shielding or knockback resistance, you’ll have some fun here. If you’re like me and you tend to rely on set-and-forget general-purpose builds, you’ll run into some roadblocks.

Other than that, you might know already whether or not you want to check it out. There’s a lot of care and art in Aether & Iron, mixed with a unique science-fiction setting that isn’t quite like anything else in video games at the moment.
Aether & Iron is currently available for PC and Mac via Steam for $24.99. Seismic Squirrel plans to release the game for PlayStation and Xbox in 2027.

articles.title: FCC clears SpaceX to put up to a million satellites in orbit for Starmind data center network
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to send up to a million satellites into orbit for its Starmind data-processing network.

In a news release , the FCC touted today’s decision as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space” and echoed the high-flown language that SpaceX used to describe the network in its application 10 months ago .
“It promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization — one that can harness the full power of the sun,” the agency said.
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the plan “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”

Carr signaled that he was all in on the Trump administration’s support for rapid data center expansion, despite a growing backlash that figured in this month’s midterm elections. He said that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership” in artificial intelligence.
“By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” Carr said.
In a post to X , SpaceX CEO Elon Musk told Carr that his praise was “much appreciated.”
“This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk said.

Proponents of solar-powered orbital data centers say such constellations will address the top concerns about terrestrial data centers, including land use, power consumption and water requirements for cooling. Critics point to the engineering challenges, including concerns about cooling the satellites, managing space traffic and dealing with orbital debris.

In approving SpaceX’s application, the FCC rejected opposition from Amazon and Viasat, as well as from the American Astronomical Society, which raised concerns about the constellation’s impact on the night sky. The AAS said in a statement that it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s decision.
The FCC attached several conditions to its authorization , including requirements for communications backups, regular updates and a detailed plan for orbital debris mitigation.

SpaceX was cleared to operate its satellites at orbits ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers (310 to 623 miles) in altitude. The first satellite is to be put into operation no later than 2033, and the FCC calls for the full constellation to be operating by 2040.

In August, SpaceX announced that it was partnering with Nvidia to design the compute payload for the Starmind AI1 satellite. “Each of the Starmind satellites will include Nvidia Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs for datacenter-class space compute,” SpaceX said at the time.

SpaceX’s facility in Redmond, Wash., makes the satellites for the Starlink telecommunications network — but in a filing related to this year’s initial public offering , SpaceX said its operation in Bastrop, Texas, would be put in charge of producing AI compute satellites.
The FCC said it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals and intends to issue decisions on each proposal “according to the agency’s regular procedures.”

articles.title: Elevated line to Ballard
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: At the Ballard Town Hall meeting somebody asked whether Sound Transit had considered elevating the line instead of tunneling to reduce cost and build it earlier. Sound Transit’s response was that they cannot imagine any way to build an elevated Link light rail line through downtown and meet current environmental requirements. An elevated line would certainly be cheaper and faster to build and easier for riders to access than the currently planned deep tunnel. Could any of the alternative modes I described make it possible to build an elevated line through downtown?

As Kubly/Reed recently pointed out, current Link trains needs very long stations. That makes it difficult to find a location for an underground station which does not interfere with existing building foundations, but also to fit an elevated station into the existing street valleys. For more infrequent lines, the station also has to allow sufficient waiting area requiring wider platforms. As Kubly/Reed pointed out, automated light metro systems allow more frequent but shorter trains which reduces the size of the station area. Link also requires a pole for overhead wires, an emergency and maintenance walkway, and potentially noise barriers along its guideway for a total width of about 29 feet . Link’s maximum turn radius (82 feet) and maximum grade (6%) also create challenges to fit the guideway into downtown. Monorail guideways are visually less bulky but still require a separate emergency walkway. When the Monorail Project suggested running the Green Line through downtown as an elevated line, people were also concerned about their privacy as riders may peek into their windows. Link would require an even wider guideway than the monorail.

Modern guideways such as used by TSB Maglev integrate the emergency walkway into the middle of the track rather than between the two tracks and only require a 20 feet wide guideway. With a center platform, a station requires a width of 50 feet (60′ for Link). To scale Seattle’s hills, grades of up to 10% can be handled. Construction is much faster and less disruptive as the guideway is prefabricated. Once the columns are built, the guideway gets trucked in and placed by crane.
Various elevated alignments have been considered in the past (or should be):

Modern maglev guideway technology may also make it feasible to run along 15th Ave W through Interbay and use precast modules for a station above the road. As such technology also allows for grades up to 10%, it may even allow a bridge over the ship canal. Otherwise a ship canal tunnel would still be required unless Sound Transit would consider a Salmon Bay gondola for now and save even more.

The downtown alignments could also be used to connect with the West Seattle line. The First Hill alignments would create a great alternative if the current downtown tunnel is out of service, with transfers at Westlake and Mt. Baker.
Elevated guideways also make it much easier to add branches (for example to serve Aurora Ave) or add a station later – practically impossible in case of a drilled tunnel.

While an elevated line would be far cheaper, it would probably require a new EIS submission. That would add a few years to the timeline, but because of the lower cost, construction could start immediately once federal approval has been obtained. That may still allow an opening date closer to the 2032 target date than waiting until 2060 and we would not have to burden our grandchildren with paying off a much larger debt.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Emerald City Trail Is an Ideal Guide to Seattle’s Olmsted History
articles.author: Valentina Vaneeva
paras: While our region is famous for its beautiful outdoors, driving for an hour or more or carrying a backpack should not be a prerequisite for taking a nice long walk and enjoying the views. But figuring out where to go in the city is sometimes frustrating if you want to avoid getting stuck in a rut, with every intersection presenting yet another choice. And so it is always a joy when a new guidebook falls into your hands.

Emerald City Trail: A Walking Guide Through Seattle & Our Olmsted History , written by Peter Hendrickson of Seattle Mountaineers and published this year by Mountaineers Books, is unique in its goal of not just making your life easier by giving you directions but also tying the routes to one particular piece of Seattle history: its connection to Olmsted Brothers , heirs of the Olmsted of New York’s Central Park fame.

It is not a history book, but it gives enough of an overview of how the brothers played a role in shaping the city, and there is enough to keep your walks interesting. For those who want to learn more, the Resources section at the end of the book will be helpful.

Emerald City Trail is a 75-mile loop connecting both existing and proposed parks and boulevards that were elements of the plan developed by Olmsted Brothers for the City of Seattle at the start of the 20th century. The whole loop is conveniently split into 12 segments, 5 to 7.5 miles long, with options to shorten or lengthen any one of them, and their start and end points are accessible by transit. The guidebook also recommends detours for those with a stroller if the original route has stairs or difficult terrain.

Each section's description has a route map with viewpoints and landmarks and lists the usual stats of distance, elevation, and difficulty, but what sets this guidebook apart is that it also mentions the “Three Ts”: public transportation, public toilets and treats, that is, cafes, bakeries, bars or ice cream shops. Having such conveniences at hand lightens the load you need to carry and leaves you free to stray off route at will.

The book is of a small size and can be used for navigation directly, but you may prefer following its companion interactive map at emeraldcitytrail.com since it shows your actual location and has a built-in transit layer. Depending on your screen size, you may not find the interface very convenient and may prefer to download the GPX file of the whole loop or a segment you're interested in to be used with a navigation app of your choice.

Despite what the book says, at the time of this writing, you cannot download GPX tracks from its companion website, but they are available from the Mountaineers website ; scroll past the description and click on the “Resources” section.

This Mountaineers page also lists upcoming walks for sections of the route, so if you are looking for company or want to meet the author, you can sign up for one. Additionally, you can look up recent trip reports, and this too sets the book apart from other urban walking guidebooks because each segment has a Mountaineer steward who walks their section at least quarterly to spot safety or maintenance issues.

The guidebook also highlights difficulties walking in some parts of Seattle for which geography cannot be blamed . The route of Section 6, Rainier Beach to White Center, is the most challenging part of Emerald City Trail. Since it goes through an industrial area, there is not much shade, few restrooms and food options, but plenty of high-speed traffic and tricky highway crossings. Indeed, the author recommends avoiding the most unsafe crossing altogether and catching a bus instead, which is something you cannot do on a regular hike even if you bring your Orca transit card.
Compare that to Section 2, Woodland Park Zoo to Husky Stadium, which goes through a park and along tree-lined streets and has plenty of opportunity for treats on the way.

I am yet to complete the whole 75 miles of the loop, in fact, I have just started, but I like that the route gives you an enjoyable mix of nature, art, historic landmarks and people watching. And, as Hendrickson promised, on our very first walk, when we stopped for a coffee break, we met someone interesting to talk with.

If this sounds like something you might like, this guidebook is for you. And if not, perhaps fantastic photos by Heidi Walker will inspire you to explore one of the sections. And don't let the Big Dark scare you into staying home. Worst case, you can always take a bus or a train and bail out, just don't forget your Orca card!

articles.title: a-ha’s Morten Harket: ‘My Parkinson’s diagnosis wasn’t devastating. I have a new appreciation for the human organism’
articles.author: As told to Magnus Nome
paras: As the Norwegian pop trio’s frontman releases his new album Human Grace, he answers your questions on the devastating effects of fame, living in squalor in London, 80s nostalgia – and a certain bandmate’s denim underwear

You ’ ve described your new album, Human Grace, as revealing more of yourself than your previous work. Was there anything you found unexpectedly difficult to express through these songs, or anything that surprised you about yourself during the creative process? BarefootJax No. It’s an exploratory process, the activity of making new music. It’s about quieting yourself, being available to hear tiny little differences in vibes, to pick up a seed that will blossom into something – and then it goes from being nothing to becoming a thing, instantaneously. That has never changed for me. With a-ha, there wasn’t much time and peace for songwriting. Being the frontman takes a lot of focus.

What has changed is my access to the skilled tools – singing and guitar – due to the Parkinson’s medication side-effects. For this album, we found old recordings of my voice, some from over 10 years back. It hasn’t been devastating for me to get this diagnosis – it has been a blunt and impactful instrument to stop everything I was doing. I had to reassemble myself first, to understand what it is. Losing access to parts of myself I’ve taken for granted all my life, but also a new appreciation for the architecture of ourselves as an organism – it’s so impressive. It’s mind-blowing.

articles.title: Etzioni on AI: 18 ways to use AI this Thanksgiving
articles.author: Oren Etzioni
paras: Here are 18 creative ways to use AI this Thanksgiving. Some save you time in the kitchen or at the airport, and others aim to make the meal more fun. The don’ts at the end could save your turkey, and my very last suggestion is perhaps the best.
Flight delay forecasting. Apps like Flighty (start with free tier) use machine learning to predict whether your flight will leave on time and why it might not.
Cancellation playbook drafted in advance. Have the backup flights and a rebooking script ready ahead of time, so a cancellation means consulting your AI instead of starting from scratch.
Airport pickup routing. Five relatives land at different times at two airports, and AI works out who drives whom. It can even send a polite request on your behalf.

A personal travel agent. Vayo (free, private beta), a new Seattle startup co-founded by my friend Mike Fridgen, connects to your inbox and pulls in your flight, hotel and restaurant confirmations. It keeps an eye on them for price drops and changes.
Oven Tetris. Give it your oven’s size, every dish’s temperature and the serving time. It works backward to a minute-by-minute schedule and flags the conflicts.

Decoding grandma’s recipe card. Photograph the card and have AI modernize it under one rule : it never invents quantities. “A pinch” stays “a pinch.” “un poco” or “ein bissl” may be translated, but not changed.
Reconstructing a lost dish. Several relatives describe a dish a late grandparent made. AI triangulates a recipe, you cook test versions, and the family votes on which one tastes right.
Pairing from the wines on hand. AI picks from bottles you actually own, and those brought over by guests, dish by dish, instead of a generic list. Last-minute fun!
Potluck dispatcher. One AI thread collects RSVPs and dish claims so you don’t end up with four green bean casseroles.
Trivia built from your own family’s facts. ChatGPT can now run it as a playable game, with answer buttons and a running score inside the conversation.

AI-prepped grandparent interview. Feed the AI what you already know and have it draft questions about the gaps. Record it, and afterward AI turns the transcript into a short illustrated booklet that’s in the mail by Christmas.

Angry Uncle rehearsal. Karin Tamerius, a political psychiatrist, built the Angry Uncle Bot , and it still runs in ChatGPT. A coach asks for your issue and your stance. You set the uncle’s temper from Annoyed to Apoplectic and choose whether he’s drunk or sober, and the coach critiques each reply before he answers.

Live interpreter for multilingual families. Put ChatGPT’s voice mode (paid plans) in the middle of the table so the great-aunt who only speaks Hebrew or Spanish is part of the conversation instead of watching it.
Friday leftover remix. Photograph the fridge and get a menu that makes Friday’s leftovers feel like a new meal.
Specific thank-you notes. Each note names what that person actually brought or said.
Photo triage. AI picks the best 20 of 400 photos and captions them in the family’s inside-joke voice.
“We missed you” letter for someone who wasn’t at the table. AI drafts it from the stories told at dinner.

Black Friday skeptic. Before you buy, check Google’s price insights , which tells you whether a price is high, low or typical for the past three months. Last year, 36% of Black Friday items showed no savings over their prices a few weeks earlier. Better yet, set a price track and let Google’s agent buy the item at eligible U.S. stores when it hits your number, after you confirm.

I consider myself an OG Black Friday skeptic. Back in 2011, I told the New York Times (gift link) that after crunching the price data at my startup Decide.com, the lowest electronics prices usually came in early December, not on Black Friday.

Don’t trust an AI turkey recipe on its own. Back in 2022, when the New York Times cooked a Thanksgiving from GPT-3 recipes, the turkey recipe called for one garlic clove for a 12-pound bird and no butter or oil. It came out dry and flavorless.

Don’t take a chatbot’s word on an airline’s rules. Air Canada’s chatbot told a grieving passenger he could claim a bereavement discount after he flew. The real policy said no, and he had to take the airline to a tribunal to collect $812 (Canadian). Check the airline’s own policy page, and screenshot what the bot tells you.

Don’t click on the deal of the century. Scammers now use AI to make fake shopping sites look legitimate, and the number of fake sites jumped 250% last holiday season, according to NordVPN . Type the retailer’s address yourself.
Don’t try to win the family argument with AI-fetched facts. Even the creator of Angry Uncle Bot says that bombarding your uncle with facts only makes him angrier. Ask questions and listen instead.
Here’s another option: give technology a rest.
Unplug from your devices and from AI, and have an AI-free, 100% human Thanksgiving.

articles.title: ‘Positive Charge’ season finale: What we learned chasing climate solutions across eight episodes
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Subscribe to Positive Charge : Apple Podcasts , Spotify , Amazon Music , All Episodes
Editor’s note: GeekWire reporter Lisa Stiffler, who covers climate and sustainability, co-hosts the Positive Charge podcast with producer Laura Scott.

We went inside a fusion lab in Everett, a jet fuel plant in Moses Lake and a factory in British Columbia giving old EV batteries a second life. We tasted plant-based chicken nuggets at 9 a.m. and stepped into a shipping container in Tacoma that destroys “forever chemicals.”

Over eight episodes, the inaugural season of the Positive Charge podcast from GeekWire went across the Pacific Northwest ( and beyond ) in search of promising climate and sustainability technologies to help humanity dig our way out of some pretty dire environmental straits.
While the challenge is huge — a warming planet, increased use of fossil fuels, toxic chemicals in our food and water — there are wide-ranging solutions out there, and many are taking hold.

On this episode, GeekWire co-founder Todd Bishop sits down with producer Laura Scott and me, the hosts of Positive Charge, to look back on the season. We explore the themes that emerged across the episodes, savor some highlights and even get a little emotional when discussing the question of whether all of it left us more hopeful about the planet.

Going behind the scenes. At Helion Energy in Everett, we got a sneak peek of a miniaturized fusion test device that was cordoned off and still under construction. To see it, we walked behind a huge plastic curtain, which Laura memorably compared to walking into the Costco dairy section.

Our podcast on alternative proteins went inside Rebellyous Foods , a startup manufacturing plant-based chicken nuggets being served in U.S. schools, as well as some medical and correctional facilities. We were offered a plate of the nuggets — which we scarfed down, despite the tour taking place first thing in the morning.
“My biggest regret of the whole season,” Laura said, “is that we did not take Rebellyous up on their offer to send us home with those chicken nuggets because you cannot buy them in stores.”

The importance of large, committed customers. A lot of these technologies are expensive propositions, from R&D to prototypes to scaling. “Having a willing and able corporate buyer is something that can really spark the innovation to happen,” Todd observed.

That includes Microsoft’s agreement to buy power from Helion , purchase agreements for sustainable aviation fuel from Twelve and Montana Renewables , and Redwood Materials ‘ deal to supply used EV batteries to power a data center for Crusoe . Rebellyous built its business on school lunch programs.

The essential role of organizations coming together collectively to support new sustainable technologies was a key message of a New York Climate Week panel, where I interviewed Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, and Jason Knauf, CEO of The Earthshot Prize.
We discussed the fact that when customers commit, it unlocks investments to scale production. That in turn lowers costs for everything from faux nuggets to cleaner jet fuel.

AI is driving the money. The data centers behind the AI boom are often cast as a threat to tech companies’ climate goals. In several episodes, they were also a reason for money to flow into clean energy.
“There’s so much money going into environmental solutions because of data centers,” Laura said. “It’s a catalyst for funding. It’s a catalyst for fusion.”
There’s money to be made. While many sustainability entrepreneurs are fundamentally mission-driven, they’re also focused on the fiscal bottom line and so are venture capitalists.

At Pacific Northwest Climate Week , Laura was struck by how enthusiastic investors are about the space, and not only because they want to save the planet. They’re “entirely self-interested,” she said, “and that’s what gave me hope.”
PNW is a sustainability hub. In each episode of Positive Charge, we toured a Pacific Northwest startup, plus we interviewed related companies outside the area and sector experts.

The local companies included Helion and Zap Energy in Everett, Aquagga in Tacoma, Sedron Technologies in Sedro-Woolley, Twelve in Moses Lake, Rebellyous in Seattle and Moment Energy in British Columbia.

The range of topics reinforced the region’s standing as a hub for sustainable tech, including batteries, fusion, aviation, environmental cleanup, and even potentially overlooked fields, such as end-of-life services.
Laura’s unexpected favorite episode was about startups offering human composting as a green alternative to burial or cremation, and Todd ranked it a close second (his No. 1 was EV battery reuse).

Seattle is home to Recompose — the first U.S. company to offer the service after its founder, Katrina Spade, spearheaded the effort in 2019 to make the practice legal. Since then, human composting startups Return Home and Earth Funeral have also launched in the Seattle area.
After exploring all of these technologies and talking to entrepreneurs, investors and leaders in the space, Todd asked if we were more or less hopeful for the planet.
“Definitely more hopeful,” Laura said. “I didn’t expect to feel more hopeful, though. I expected to feel about the same, or maybe a little bit worse.”

But seeing the financial case for these solutions helped shift her thinking. One example is Sedron, which is treating sewage waste with a technology that destroys PFAS forever chemicals and also generates enough clean electricity that the excess can be sold to others. Laura was impressed by the opportunity to do right by the environment while creating revenue.

I hover between hope and anxiety. But after years of covering these issues, I appreciated a sentiment shared by Earthshot finalist Franco Rodríguez Viau, CEO and co-founder of Satellites on Fire, who said he needs to do everything he can to tackle climate change, whether or not humanity succeeds in reaching its goals.
That’s how I feel about covering climate. As I mentioned on the show, I don’t know if I feel hopeful, “but I can’t feel indifferent. I have to show up and do this.”
Positive Charge is a GeekWire podcast sponsored by Amazon Sustainability.

articles.title: Meta’s teen restrictions have a gap: TikTok, Snapchat and YouTube leave teens room to scroll
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Meta’s new teen restrictions, set to take effect by late February, could meaningfully curb endless scrolling. A new study suggests they probably won’t.

That’s because the restrictions, which are part of a settlement between Meta and dozens of attorneys general, including Washington’s, apply only to Instagram and Facebook. They leave out Snapchat, TikTok and Google-owned YouTube.

“The simple workaround right now is that you just switch platforms, and we already know that teens are on three to four platforms on average,” said Dr. Dimitri Christakis, a principal investigator at the Center for Child Health, Behavior and Development at Seattle Children’s .

Christakis led research published Wednesday showing Instagram and Facebook accounted for roughly 20% of total daily social media use for youth. So when the restrictions kick in, teens could just shift to other platforms.

The rules establish a two-hour daily limit combined across Instagram and Facebook, restrict access to content from midnight to 6 a.m., and mute most school-hour push notifications. Parents can adjust the protections, and direct messaging is exempt.
If the same limits were applied across the five most popular platforms, that could make a dent in teen usage, according to the research letter in the Journal of the American Medical Association .
In an analysis of recorded app activity from 1,803 adolescent Android users, the researchers estimated:
The study has no way of knowing how teens will respond to the restrictions or the impacts on their health. It simply estimates how much previously recorded activity would fall under the rules.

The researchers disclosed ties to social media litigation. Christakis reported paid legal consulting work, including for Washington’s attorney general, and co-author Lauren Hale of Stony Brook University reported fees for serving as an expert witness. The third author is Yihong Zhao of Columbia University.
Despite the limited benefits of the coming restrictions, Christakis said they’re a “step in the right direction.”

“Let’s say it’s an incremental improvement. It’s clearly not going to be enough by itself because of what our study found,” he said. “But these are the right kinds of restrictions. We need to make them universal, and we need to enforce them.”
Meta, not surprisingly, is in favor of having the restrictions apply industry wide.
When the settlement was announced in August the company issued a statement saying that “ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative.”
Meta called on others to do the same: “For meaningful progress to happen, we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this new standard…”

The agreement resolves claims by 48 states, Washington, D.C., and U.S. territories that Meta designed addictive platforms and failed to protect young users, among other allegations. Meta did not admit wrongdoing.

In addition to the safety changes, Meta agreed to pay participating governments up to $17.1 billion over a decade, according to Washington’s attorney general. Washington will receive at least $237 million and could receive nearly $339 million.

The higher settlement is unlocked only if TikTok and YouTube adopt similar protections and make payments of their own, according to Meta. If that happens, additional restrictions kick in, curbing access on all the platforms from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m.
Those additional hours are significant. The researchers found nearly as much use between 10 p.m. and midnight as during the entire midnight-to-6-a.m. window covered by the initial limits.

Whether the other companies will follow remains unclear. All five social media platforms are named in additional legal challenges alleging harm to youth, Reuters reported, including suits filed by individuals, school districts and municipalities.

In September, TikTok reached its first settlement in a state-led case, agreeing to teen usage restrictions in Alabama and a payment of at least $100 million, according to Reuters. YouTube CEO Neal Mohan, meanwhile, dismissed joining Meta’s agreement and emphasized his company’s own safety efforts, CNN reported.

Christakis said both time spent on social media and the platforms’ features can exacerbate problems involving sleep, mental health, body image and attention. He hopes the growing body of research translates into action.

“I’m not a legislator, and I’m not an advocate. I’m a scientist that’s really trying to make sure that we apply science in the best interests of our children’s health,” he said. “And in this space, in particular, we haven’t been doing that.”

articles.title: Sound Transit Debuts Refurbished Kinkisharyo Link Trains
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: This morning, Sound Transit quietly launched the first refurbished Kinkisharyo trainset on the 2 Line. After years of design and months of testing, light-rail vehicles 110 and 113 ran a roundtrip between Redmond and Lynnwood during the morning rush hour. Part of the initial Link fleet delivered in 2006, these vehicles have been out of service for a deep refurbishment that saw upgrades to the train’s electrical and communication systems.

In 2022, Sound Transit contracted Woojin IS America to refresh the 62 Kinkisharyo trains, also knows as Series 1. These trains were delivered between 2006 and 2011 and include some now-outdated components. Replacing these will allow the vehicles to remain in a state of good repair for the next 15 years. Many of the upgrades are out-of-sight from passengers, including new operator controls, automated passenger counters (APC) in every car, upgraded CCTV cameras, and an ethernet-based networking system.

Passengers will notice a few changes on the refurbished KI trains. The exterior-facing displays now show the line color and number. Inside the train, the dot matrix displays have been replaced by the screens that show the next few stops. These screens are slightly different from those on Series 2 trains, and do not show connections to other transit routes. Three lights have been added around each door. The lights flash blue when the door will open soon and change color to green when the door is open. The onboard speakers have been upgraded to provide clearer announcements. These trains also allow the Link Control Center to make remote announcements when needed. A video of the PA system and door lights in action is available here .

Four of the 62 Series 1 LRVs have completed the retrofit and two more are currently undergoing the retrofit process. The remaining 56 LRVs will be upgraded over the next three years. Retrofitted LRVs are not compatible with original Series 1 LRVs, so the number of upgraded trainsets in use will be limited until more cars complete the retrofitting process. For the foreseeable future, expect to see the new trains Monday-Friday on block 53 in the morning and block 54 in the afternoon. For the exact timings of each block, refer to the schedule on Pantograph .

articles.title: Rebecca Saldaña Joins King County Council
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Rebecca Saldaña was sworn in Tuesday as the newest member of the King County Council, a new representative for District 2, which spans South and Central Seattle, Skyway, the U District, and Ravenna. Saldaña took office immediately after this November's election was certified, taking over for Rhonda Lewis, who had been appointed to fill the council seat vacated by King County Executive Girmay Zahilay last fall.

A former state senator who has represented the 37th Legislative District since 2016, Saldaña joins a legislative body that continues to battle an array of challenges, including a growing structural deficit in the county's general fund, escalating costs on capital projects, and a looming fiscal cliff for the state's largest transit agency.

Saldaña campaigned on a populist message of taxing the "ultra-wealthy," but King County is famously constrained in the type of taxes that it can levy. State law bars counties from implementing the type of revenue tools available to Washington cities including taxes on business & occupation, utilities, capital gains, or payroll.

"I want to thank the voters of District 2, who have seen my service and chose to send me to the front lines to make sure we are protecting our local democracy, and making sure that we're demonstrating that when people we believe in people, when we believe in ourselves, we can make government work for all of us, especially and particularly for those that are on the margins," Saldaña said in a speech following her swearing-in.

In an election that pitted her against Port of Seattle Commissioner Toshiko Hasegawa, daylight was often hard to discern between the two candidates. Nonetheless, Saldaña was ultimately able to easily consolidate Seattle progressives behind her campaign, earning the endorsements of both The Stranger and The Urbanist (on whose elections committee I serve) – in addition to a slew of state legislators and a majority of labor unions, which won her the sole nod from the MLK Labor Council.

Hasegawa earned the endorsement of the Seattle Times, and ended up only seeing majority support in District 2's wealthier areas including Madison Park, Laurelhurst, and the Rainier Valley's waterfront areas. Hasegawa pulled in endorsements from some big name politicians, including Zahilay and former governors Jay Inslee and Gary Locke.
In the end, Saldaña secured 61.5% of the vote against Hasegawa.

Saldaña is expected to bring an organizer's perspective to the County Council, with a deep background in labor advocacy prior to serving in elected office. She told The Urbanist that her top priorities would be affordable housing, safer and healthier communities, and economic empowerment.

"I want to lower costs and expand opportunity through reliable transit, childcare, infrastructure, and good union jobs," Saldaña wrote in a response to The Urbanist elections committee's questionnaire this summer. "Housing, climate, transit, and public health are deeply connected, and I believe King County must continue leading on progressive revenue so working families are not paying a larger share of their income in taxes than the wealthiest among us."

A year into a shortened three-year term, Executive Zahilay has largely received deference from the County Council on implementing his administration's priorities, including a major restructuring of the Executive's Office that sent many long-time civil servants packing. This week, Zahilay told the Seattle Times that those moves were intended to set up "bigger impacts next year," but so far he has shied away from launching major policy initiatives, apart from signaling support for a countywide housing levy in 2027.

One area where Saldaña has distinguished herself from sitting councilmembers is by pushing back on Zahilay's three-day return-to-office (RTO) mandate , which is slowly being phased in as the County spends on office renovations. The mandate has been unpopular with workers, who argue that county officials aren't providing satisfactory accommodations for individual circumstances.

Saldaña took office just minutes after approval of a supplemental budget that allocates $18.7 million to office renovations at the King County Administration Building and the Dexter Horton Building needed to enable the RTO mandate to continue being implemented.

"I do not support blanket return-to-office mandates that are not grounded in service delivery, worker needs, equity, cost, and operational reality. King County should be a strong public employer that respects workers’ time, family responsibilities, disability accommodations, commute burdens, and recruitment and retention challenges," Saldaña wrote in her Urbanist questionnaire response. "If in-person work improves public access or service delivery, departments should make thoughtful decisions based on operational needs. But broad mandates that create additional workspace costs and reduce flexibility without clear public benefit do not make sense."

Saldaña's speech on Tuesday sounded a hopeful note, after giving words of praise to Lewis – the first Black woman ever to serve on the King County Council. Saldaña's presence maintains the council as majority female, and increases its Latino/Latina bloc to a full third of councilmembers.

"We can meet people where they're at and not leave them there. We can actually bring everyone in, and it is here in King County that we will be leading and giving hope not only to our neighbors but to our nation and to our world. Our future is now," Saldaña said.
Saldaña concluded her speech Tuesday with the motto of the United Farm Workers of America, a clear nod to the start of her own career as an organizer with Oregon's farmworkers union: "Si se puede."

articles.title: King County Metro Pushes Back Seattle Bus Service Restoration
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seattle transit riders are set to wait longer for promised bus service increases, as King County Metro pushes back planned service restorations within the city that had been on deck for 2027. Over the course of the year, 114,000 hours of new bus service has been in the works for years as part of the agency's Covid-19 service recovery plan .
But now, that service won't hit the streets until 2028, King County Metro officials confirmed with The Urbanist this week.

This Seattle service ramp-up is separate from increases planned thanks to the Seattle Transit Measure, which voters approved in a beefed-up form this month by a landslide 73% . Rather, the Seattle Service Recovery Project is set to look at routes that still remain suspended – mostly peak-only routes like the Route 15 to Ballard's Blue Ridge neighborhood and the Route 37 to Alki – and how to bring service back in those areas in a way that's more in alignment with the current vision for an all-day, frequent network across the city.

With service restorations already implemented in South King County, North King County, and on the Eastside, Seattle has remained on Metro's to-do list along with adjustments planned in Renton . Now the timeline to implement those changes is stretching.

"Metro does intend to restore the full 114,000 hours of service in Seattle. However, we have had a shift in the timing of those hours," Katie Chalmers, Metro's Service Development Managing Director, told The Urbanist. "They were initially budgeted for 2027, but since the time that that budget was developed, we have shifted the project later."
This delay will likely mean it takes longer to return to 2019-level bus service in Seattle, with Metro currently providing around 92% of the service hours that were provided seven years ago.

Chalmers said that implementing the Seattle Transit Measure – which will ramp up to an additional 95,000 service hours across the city – will be Metro's primary task in 2027, with engagement around which routes to invest in with the 114,000 hours set to kick off early next year.

"The Seattle Recovery Project would have looked really different if Prop 1 had been sized differently, or if it had not passed. So, together with the City of Seattle, we made the determination that we would shift the timeline later," Chalmers said. "We'll engage with the public and with the mobility board and others through the first half of next year, and we'll transmit an ordinance to the Council in early 2028, with most of the changes expected to happen in August 2028."

The delay to broader service restoration could lessen the sense of victory for transit advocates who fought for more funding, and didn't necessarily expect it to come at the expense of other planned service increases. Riders may prefer faster service restoration rather than two years of engagement and outreach process to dissect the particulars of the decision.
The Seattle Transit Measure hours set to roll out next year are likely to be on existing routes, beefing up all-day frequency in service of filling gaps particularly on nights and weekends.

In 2022, the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) established an equity-centered "Investment Prioritization Methodology" in coordination with the City's Transit Advisory Board, a framework that is much more likely to prioritize areas in South Seattle and the Duwamish Valley.
A map shown to councilmembers this summer highlighted likely contenders for investments given the STM's passage, and no peak-only or suspended routes were shown.

But some City leaders have been pushing for Metro to move more quickly to restore suspended service in underserved areas. A budget amendment put forward this month by Councilmember Dan Strauss (whose District 6 includes Ballard and Magnolia) would have squirreled away $2.5 million for the Route 15, along with the Route 17, which currently only runs four roundtrips every weekday up 32nd Avenue NW. Strauss referenced the above map in making comments in support of the amendment, which would mean that SDOT couldn't be able to tab the funding for any other corridors.

"SDOT slides themselves demonstrated that Ballard does not benefit from the same frequency that other parts of the city do, and what they didn't show was the travel times, which are comparable to traveling from downtown Seattle to Tacoma," Strauss said.

Strauss's statement isn't exactly true: Sound Transit's 594 bus takes around an hour to get from the start of its route in Downtown Seattle to Tacoma Dome during peak hours, while the D Line only takes around 35 minutes to reach 15th Avenue NW and NW Market Street.

"I wouldn't bring this amendment if it wasn't a regional growth center. If it wasn't a place where the city has chosen to put density but has chosen not to put the transit service that is comparable to other parts of our city," Strauss added.

The amendment was defeated on a 3-6 vote, with Councilmembers Hollingworth and Kettle voting in favor. In speaking against, Councilmember Dionne Foster cited a memo produced by SDOT that outlined potential transit service investments that are likely to get STM funding, and which would otherwise be put on the back burner if Strauss's amendment passed. Notably, the list did not include any Ballard routes.

"Seeing routes in districts 1, 2, 3, 7, 4, 5 and 6, it feels to me like we are sort of putting that ahead of the work that the department needs to do," Foster said. "I think it's important that we have the [regional] transit centers as part of the prioritization criteria, but I don't believe that we should be provisoing this resource ahead of the county taking on their service realignment work."

Strauss's push isn't likely to go away, especially as he heads into reelection in 2027. But County Councilmembers are likely going to have opinions of their own on how transit investments should be made in their district. On Tuesday, the County Council approved an amendment from Councilmember Jorge Barón to its own budget that puts a hold on $4.16 million in funding to implement service changes next fall. That dollar amount is associated with 50,000 annual service hours.
Barón and Strauss's districts heavily overlap, with Barón also representing Queen Anne, South Lake Union, and Belltown – but their priorities may not.

"We've been patiently waiting since the pandemic and the restoration [of] service because our region has been the last one to get the restructure," Barón said earlier this month in committee. "Because our district has been, my district in particular, has been patiently waiting for years for this, and especially because of the Sound Transit decision earlier this year not to fund full construction to Ballard , there is an added level of interest and urgency in District 4 to make sure that that happens on the timeline that had been proposed before."
But Chalmers shied away from saying that Metro would be ready to put additional buses on the road by that timeline as part of the Seattle Service Recovery Plan.

"If by the point that we're making decisions for the fall, we are ready to add more service administratively, Metro can use those funds that are encumbered by the legislation. So, we do feel like we that, while we can't commit to that right at this moment, we feel like we are comfortable with that restriction. And we hear the strong interest in delivering as much service as possible quickly," Chalmers said. "We are just going to have to work through our engagement and figure out whether we want to go ahead and try and put some hours in in the fall, or we would hold the balance."

And then there's the issue of Metro's looming fiscal cliff , set to become evident in the early 2030s as the agency continues to draw down its financial reserves. Chalmers said that's not yet a part of the conversation around service restoration, which raises the question of being able to expand service without a clear long-term picture of how to maintain it.

"Right now, Metro's financial problem is several years out in terms of when we would be looking at planning to respond. There's a lot of different elements that could change the trajectory of Metro's finances," Chalmers said. "We have not begun any sort of specific service planning related to reducing the system, but it's definitely in our view as something we've got to be ready for. Right now, our commitment really is to see the service recovery through in Seattle and in Renton. These are commitments that we've made to our communities and to riders. So that is our immediate focus."

articles.title: Seattle and King County join court fight to block I-638 before December rollout
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: You view the J. Doe A, et al. v. State of Washington complaint here (PDF)
Seattle and King County have filed a joint amicus brief asking a court to block I-638, joining a widening local legal pushback in support of a lawsuit filed by parents and student-athletes.

Seattle and King County have made the filing to support a motion for a preliminary injunction, asking the court to immediately halt the implementation and enforcement of I-638 before its December 3 effective date while the underlying lawsuit proceeds.

Filed in King County Superior Court by several Washington families alongside advocacy groups and the Washington Education Association , the lawsuit is challenging the voter-approved initiative for banning transgender girls from K–12 female sports and requiring all female student-athletes to undergo medical verification of their biological sex.

Represented by the ACLU of Washington, Legal Voice, and Pacifica Law Group , the plaintiffs argue the measure violates the state constitution and its Equal Rights Amendment, right to privacy, and guarantee of equal access to public education.

Seattle Public Schools has not joined the lawsuit but is participating as a “friend of the court,” allowing it to join the effort to pause the law before it disrupts winter sports, arguing that enforcing the rules mid-season would disrupt school sports and create legal confusion.

While Washington voters approved I-638 with 56% of the vote, it was rejected in Seattle and King County, where only 42% of ballots supported it. Advocacy groups quickly mobilized for a court battle after early returns showed little room for a statewide reversal. The Capitol Hill-based Gender Justice League noted that late campaign funding hindered broad grassroots voter education and warned of the measure’s sweeping scope, stating, “I-638 was sold as a rule about a handful of Trans youth, when in reality, it’s a medical sex check for every girl playing school sports in this state — whether Trans or not.”

In their filing, Seattle and King County argue that I-638 violates the Washington Constitution’s equal protection safeguards by establishing different rules for boys’ and girls’ sports, as well as privacy protections by mandating “physically invasive and sparsely defined medical evaluations.” Local leaders also contend the initiative clashes directly with Seattle’s antidiscrimination laws and King County’s Charter and Code protections prohibiting discrimination based on sex, gender identity, or gender expression.

“This ballot initiative was poorly written, misleading, and conflicts with local law. Specifically, it puts state law in conflict with local laws in Seattle and King County, and it violates the Washington Constitution that I swore an oath to defend,” Seattle City Attorney Erika Evans said in a statement.
Unless blocked by an injunction, officials warn the measure will disrupt local athletic facilities, weaken school-based health centers, and create compliance hurdles as winter sports get underway.

In a message sent to families Monday, Seattle Public Schools outlined the steps student-athletes participating in girls’ sports must take to comply with new Washington Interscholastic Activities Association eligibility rules.

While noting that the district had asked the WIAA to postpone implementation until the spring season because the initiative “presents operational challenges for schools,” SPS said its commitment to keeping athletes eligible and reaffirmed its stance on campus climate. “We also remain committed to an inclusive school community where every student is welcomed, respected, and supported,” the message read.

Under the guidance, students who already have a valid athletic physical on file must have an approved healthcare provider — such as an MD, DO, ARNP, PA, or ND — sign a separate WIAA Attestation Form, while those needing a new physical must use an updated form that incorporates the biological sex verification. Students without the documentation on file will be barred from competing in contests, though they will still be permitted to practice, SPS said.

articles.title: Seattle looks to neighborhood stories to guide plans for reconnecting Capitol Hill across I-5
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Seattle residents will have new ways to help shape a plan for reconnecting neighborhoods divided by I-5 including Capitol Hill, Eastlake, and downtown. Led by the Seattle Office of Planning and Community Development , the Reconnecting Communities Across I-5 project is launching public engagement activities to gather resident feedback and establish the priorities guiding future work.
The study area stretches from South Lake Union to the Chinatown International District, spanning four City Council districts and seven neighborhoods.

The effort builds on decades of city history and grassroots organizing around the highway’s impact on Seattle. When I-5 was built in the 1960s, it displaced homes and businesses and cut downtown off from eastern neighborhoods like Capitol Hill and First Hill, leaving nearby residents facing ongoing pollution, noise, and physical barriers. The construction also sparked the historic Seattle Freeway Revol — a protest movement that stopped later freeway expansions from tearing through the Central District.

Out of that era came Seattle’s original freeway cap, Freeway Park , which opened on July 4, 1976. Designed by Lawrence Halprin & Associates , the park was created as an open green space to physically bridge the divide between downtown, First Hill, and Capitol Hill.
In the decades since, neighbors and advocates have pushed to build on that model and quiet the roar of the freeway — while also creating new neighborhoods above the busy interstate.

Starting in 2010, the citizen-led Lid I-5 group began holding community design workshops to picture covering sections of the highway between Madison and Thomas streets with parks, schools, affordable housing, and shops, effectively creating new land in the heart of Seattle.

That push gained major support at City Hall and the state level in recent years, backed by a 2020 feasibility study that found strong potential to bridge the corridor, a 2023 Seattle City Council resolution formally endorsing I-5 lid planning, and nearby state projects like the Montlake Lid and the Roanoke Lid construction.

Supported by $2.2 million in state and federal funding for planning and technical analysis, the city’s 2026–2028 visioning phase will guide future environmental review, design, and construction, even as advocates also push for repairs and fountain restorations at the aging Freeway Park.

Residents can get involved now through the Office of Planning and Community Development’s new virtual Library of Stories , open for submissions through January 2027. People are invited to visit powerofconnection.participate.online to share what makes them feel most connected to their neighborhood and browse reflections submitted by others.

Looking ahead to early 2027, the city will host The Power of Connection , a four-part January event series exploring movement, gathering, time, and nature through art and storytelling. Residents and local groups can spread the word using the partner toolkit and sign up for project alerts at seattle.gov .

articles.title: The Best Restaurants and Bars at Sea-Tac International Airport (SEA)
articles.author: <name>Meg van Huygen</name>
paras: Both locals and frequent flyers know that it’s okay to arrive hungry when you’re traveling to Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), because across its terminals, travelers can find more than 60 spots to eat and drink, from exquisite (or at least palatable) coffee to sit-down dinners. In 2026, the long-awaited C Concourse expansion finally finished and reopened, introducing 13 new dining options, and there are fresh selections in the other concourses, too. Whether you’re looking for Mexican street food, Hawaiian fare, PNW-French fusion, or Southern barbecue — or just something pleasant-tasting to carry you to the gate — this guide will help you choose based on what you’re craving, where you’re departing from, and how much time you think you have.
For a more comprehensive list of airport dining options, check out Explore SEA’s official website . This list was last updated in November 2026.
No matter where you’re traveling, make sure to create an Eater account or download the Eater app for iOS to discover great restaurant recommendations in your area and create your own guides.

Lucky Louie Fish Shack The house specialty here is sustainable Alaskan pollock and salmon, served classically (that is, battered and deep-fried with chips). The fish tacos are a mélange of Pacific Rim flavors: crispy Baja-style salmon, sesame slaw, pickled red onions, and creamy sriracha sauce. Other solid picks include clam chowder, honey teriyaki salmon, and taiyaki, a fish-shaped waffle stuffed with cheesecake filling.

BrewTop Social If you’re early for a flight, this is the place to kill time — the main attraction here is the second-story view of the airfield, and the secondary attraction is the range of beer and cocktails. They also serve breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

Co-owners Elonka and Martin Perez opened their newest location of Taco Street in 2026 after being selected as one of the first recipients of the Port of Seattle’s small-business incubator program from a pool of dozens of hopeful vendors. This family-run taqueria serves Mexican favorites made with slow-cooked meats like carne asada, barbacoa, al pastor, and pollo. Vegetarian fillings like potato, elote, and soyrizo are also available. Quesabirria tacos are available either as singles or a trio, and carne asada fries come dressed with pico de gallo, sour cream, and guac. There’s also burritos — in breakfast and non-breakfast formats — ceviche, mangonadas, and five different agua fresca flavors made fresh daily.

Salty’s at the SEA If you have time for a sit-down meal, this branch of West Seattle seafood destination Salty’s on Alki has a wide range of breakfast, lunch, and dinner options as well as an oyster bar — plus a display that shows Salty’s waterfront views on sunny days. Beats the (probably) rainy sky.

Floret At the intersection of Concourses A and B, next to the Delta Lounge, this spin-off of renowned Seattle vegetarian restaurant Cafe Flora serves a totally meat-free menu. Dishes include brioche breakfast sandwiches, seasonal veggie scrambles, and pastries, like Flora’s popular vegan cinnamon rolls. Floret has plenty of lunch and dinner options, too, such as grain bowls, salads, and a black bean burger.

Mi Casa Cantina This colorful Tex-Mex bar-resto is a solid choice for nachos, tacos, and burritos, and the guac is a crowd fave. It also has an extensive cocktail menu that showcases tequila and mezcal, and there’s even a selection of frozen margs. They make a fine paloma too.

LouLou Market and Bar Thierry Rautureau, Seattle’s famous “Chef in the Hat,” died in 2023 . After a storied career, his last remaining restaurant is LouLou Market and Bar, featuring dishes like salade Niçoise, a prime rib French dip sandwich, and crepes.

Nanny’s: A Northwest BBQ Joint (C Gate) Bringing a local take on down-home barbecue to the sometimes shi-shi C Concourse, Nanny’s is doing Southern smoked meats with some Northwestern tweaks thrown in. Plates with slow-smoked brisket, pulled pork, and pork ribs are the mains, served with cornbread, honey butter, coleslaw, and pickles. Sandwich options include pulled pork or shredded tri-tip on a sweet Hawaiian bun, topped with slaw, barbecue sauce, and crispy onions. Wings — er, “wangs” — come in sauce options like spicy barbecue or hot honey, and there are loaded waffle fries and smoked salmon chowder. The menu also includes comfort-food sides like mac and cheese or coleslaw, big salads, and even a classic Seattle dog.

Just across from Nanny’s BBQ, this pretty little teal-and-gold cocktail bar serves drinks with global flavors. Some crowd faves are the Silk Road Lychee Martini, made with vodka, lychee syrup, and fresh lime, and the Yuzu Kiss, with vodka, raspberry puree, lemon, simple syrup, and yuzu liqueur. For a nonalcoholic option, the Taipei Jasmine Fizz blends pineapple juice, jasmine tea, simple syrup, and soda. Drinks can be chased with snacks like the Bavarian pretzel charcuterie board, stacked with cured meats, artisanal cheeses, fruit, and dipping sauce, or some spinach artichoke Parmesan dip with veggie flatbread. The sausage breakfast croissant presents very luxe, too, while the bar’s Art Deco-ish stylings and white marble bartop give it a swanky feel that seems, well, appropriate in the slightly more upscale C Gates.

Dish D’Lish TV chef Kathy Casey’s grab-and-go spot is of the best places to eat in the airport for those with dietary restrictions, stocked as it is with plenty of gluten-free options. Salads include wasabi potatoes, Mediterranean quinoa, and Northwest couscous.

Hachi-ko This restaurant offers wide-ranging Asian cuisine. Diners can find hot dishes like teriyaki and chicken adobo, plus made-to-order poke bowls and heaping breakfasts with sticky rice, scrambled eggs, and Portuguese sausage for (by airport standards) a steal. There’s also a grab-and-go case with sandwiches, salads, and Spam musubis.

Le Grand Comptoir The upscale option near the C Gates is Le Grand Comptoir, French for “airport wine bar.” There’s an ample wine list that naturally features a lot of Washington wine, plus small plates, charcuterie, and tartines.

Poke to the Max A modern Seattle icon, Sam Choy’s Poke to the Max serves Hawaiian classics from early morning through late evening. Options include customizable poke bowls, loco moco topped with sunny-side-up eggs, burgers and kalua pork sandwiches on King’s Hawaiian buns, and ice cream flavors like lilikoʻi (a.k.a. passionfruit) and pineapple whip from Seattle’s own Laina’s Handcrafted Ice Cream.

Ballard Brew Hall This is your spot if you want one more brew before heading out of town. Alongside eight taps pouring craft beers, the Ballard Brew Hall also has a bloody mary menu and a wide selection of breakfast dishes, like cinnamon French toast and biscuits and gravy. (If it’s too late for breakfast, there are also flatbreads.)

Neighborhood This bubble tea shop features Filipino flavors like leche flan and turon, which is made with jackfruit and banana syrup. But even if you’re not a boba fan, it’s worth a visit for the Fulcrum coffee (Neighborhood uses it in a lovely sesame latte) and a food menu that includes croissant sandwiches and lumpia.

Seattle Dawg House This hot dog-focused sports bar (locals will get it — dogs like hot dogs and dawgs like Huskies) also serves Belgian liège waffles, replete with pearl sugar, for some reason. Other menu options include a unique take on the Seattle dog, which embellishes the original with barbecue sauce and jalapeños. Sure, why not?

Greedy Cow Burger Honestly, this area of the airport has very few dining options. For something filling, try this burger place that pairs messy burgers with triple-cooked fries. They also have Impossible burgers for the vegetarian/vegan crowd.
Moe’s Indian Kitchen The other option around the S gates is this quick-service Indian place that serves familiar dishes like chicken tikka masala.

Caffe Vita There are quite a few coffee options at SEA, it being the main airport for Seattle and all, but if you’re at all finicky about your espresso, Caffe Vita is what you want. There’s always a line, but it goes fast. The golden milk latte with turmeric, ginger, cardamom, and cinnamon (among other spices) is a luxurious favorite.

Bambuza Vietnam Kitchen and Bar This family-owned restaurant has a nice selection of Vietnamese dishes, and the portions are generous. Banh mi, pho, massive noodle and rice bowls, and bubble tea smoothies are among the highlights.

Beecher’s Handmade Cheese In addition to its namesake cheeses, this quintessential Pike Place cheesemaker has a satellite station at SEA, offering Beecher’s famous mac and cheese, hot breakfast items, and grilled sandwiches. It also has a small grab-and-go freezer stocked with Salt and Straw ice cream.

Lil Woody’s This is a well-loved Seattle burger chain famous for its collabs with notable local chefs. Though it’s best known for its milkshakes and burgs, you should be aware of the breakfast menu at this location, which features a New Mexican-style breakfast sandwich with Hatch chiles and bacon, plus bloody marys and other morning cocktails.

Skillet is an upscale diner chain that started out as a famous food truck in the 2000s ; more recently, it has closed most of its restaurants . But you can still find its breakfast-centric offerings at SeaTac Airport.
