articles.title: Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing
articles.author: Rob Davis
paras: When Oregon’s Housing Stability Council met by Zoom in early October, the state’s top housing official told the oversight board that she wanted to address a story ProPublica published that morning .

The story revealed that the official, Andrea Bell, hadn’t clearly disclosed her husband’s work for a small consulting firm that helps housing authorities develop apartments, sometimes with money from Bell’s agency. Nor had she notified Gov. Tina Kotek about it, something Oregon law requires of a governor’s appointee when an actual or potential conflict arises.

Council members, who award hundreds of millions of dollars in housing subsidies, affirmed their support for Bell, who told them she wanted to be clear: “None of the projects that are coming from the council impact my household income.”

Newly obtained records, however, show a clear financial connection between the council’s decisions and her husband’s employer. The records also show that Bell was personally involved in meetings and internal discussions about state funding of a large apartment project, Aloha 209th, which her husband’s employer is helping to develop.
Backers of the Aloha 209th project in Portland’s suburbs are seeking $17.5 million from the housing council, which receives funding recommendations from Bell’s agency.

JH Brawner, the consulting firm that employs Bell’s husband, Joshua Crites, will earn a $2 million fee from the housing authority in Washington County if the transaction closes. If not, JH Brawner gets nothing.

A separate project outside Portland, the Park Place apartments in Clackamas County, already received money through Oregon’s housing agency. Five months after Oregon awarded $36 million to the project in May 2025, Clackamas County’s housing authority paid JH Brawner a $2.4 million consulting fee, the new records show.
Like the Washington County contract, the one with Clackamas County says that if funding fell through for any reason and the project didn’t move forward, “no fee shall be due” to the firm.

JH Brawner said Crites, the firm’s director of strategic initiatives, has not worked on the Aloha 209th project but was one of five staffers assigned to Park Place. JH Brawner pays employees, including Crites, a fixed salary that is not tied to any project closing, according to managing director Zak de Gorgue.
Bell, executive director of Oregon Housing and Community Services, said in a statement that she is “committed to transparency, accountability, and compliance with state law.”

“At no point in my tenure as executive director have I used my position to influence or benefit myself or anyone related to me,” she said. “To be clear, I made no efforts to influence funding, and the Aloha 209 project has not received funding from OHCS and remains on the waitlist.”

Bell’s public agency sits in the middle of the state’s effort to combat a homelessness problem that is among the nation’s worst. Kotek, the governor, has made building more housing a pillar of her time in office. Oregon Housing and Community Services has distributed billions of state and federal dollars to subsidize the construction of apartments intended to have affordable rents.

Norman Williams, a law professor at Willamette University College of Law who teaches about government ethics, said Bell should have reported to the governor that she had a possible conflict and stayed out of any discussions about the projects her husband’s employer helped develop.
“It may all be an innocent mistake on her part,” Williams said, “but she knows who her husband is working for and she doesn’t report that. It makes it look like she’s trying to conceal this.”

De Gorgue said in a statement that the Aloha 209th project is still in development and the company had “no knowledge of Andrea Bell taking any action to move the project forward, nor has JH Brawner & Company engaged in any advocacy to secure funding approval” from Bell’s agency. Funding applications were submitted by the local housing authorities, not by JH Brawner.
“We have no indication, nor any reason to believe, that any project on which we have consulted has been the beneficiary of inappropriate influence,” de Gorgue said.
Separately, he said Clackamas and Washington counties chose JH Brawner as a consultant years before the company hired Crites in 2023.
Crites did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

After ProPublica asked Bell about her husband’s employment in September, she amended three years of ethics disclosure forms, explicitly naming JH Brawner as his employer. (The one time her state filings alluded to Crites’ job before that was in 2025, with a misspelling: “Spouse serves in an advisory role for a developmen.” It showed only the company’s street address, misspelled, and not its name.)

Bell also asked the Oregon Government Ethics Commission for a formal opinion about her potential conflict at the direction of Kotek’s staff. That evaluation was paused after the commission opened a preliminary review in response to a citizen complaint about her lack of disclosure. The preliminary review is ongoing.

ProPublica obtained the new details about Bell’s involvement through county contracts and emails to and from Bell, which were released under Oregon’s public records law. Bell’s agency initially said the emails would cost $612.50 to produce but eventually provided them for free. Washington County charged $364.25 for contracts, invoices and other documents.

Though backers say the Aloha 209th housing development is ready to be built, it’s on a waitlist to receive money from the state. Its turn is not likely to come until at least late 2028. By then, local officials worry that the delay will jeopardize its other funding sources and the project may need an even larger subsidy.

ProPublica previously reported that Molly Rogers, head of the county housing agency seeking money for Aloha 209th, spoke publicly about contacting Bell and said the state agency director was receptive to talking further.

The new records contain Bell’s recollections of the phone conversation she had with Rogers. The same morning the two spoke, in June, Bell told another department official by email that Aloha 209th had “a unique dimension of urgency and angst” because it was one of the last projects funded by a 2018 voter-approved housing bond administered by the Portland area’s Metro regional government.

Natasha Detweiler-Daby, who leads the state housing agency’s affordable rental housing division, responded to Bell that it could be “responsive and logical” to have lawmakers “add nuance” next year by dedicating some portion of funding for housing authority projects on Oregon’s waitlist. Detweiler-Daby did not respond to an email from ProPublica seeking comment.

Behind the Aloha 209th discussion was the way that Oregon awards its housing subsidies. Since 2024, Oregon has given the money on a first-come, first-served basis. When funding runs out, Bell’s agency places applications on a waitlist in the order received.

Bell spoke with Washington County officials about Aloha 209th during a 45-minute Zoom meeting in August, records show. Internal notes summarizing the conversation say that the county would send an updated report to the state agency to “inform movement of 209.” The summary said the groups involved would have a follow-up conversation about the project.

Bell went on to discuss the project with regional government officials in early September. About two weeks before the meeting, she emailed her deputy with two possible ways to get the project funded: a legislative “carve-out” or Metro consolidating its subsidies so it could fully pay for the project. “I want to do everything we can to help the metro projects be successful and the resources, like ours, are nearly depleted,” Bell wrote. She acknowledged that Metro might not find the solution appealing.
Bell told ProPublica that she met with Metro and Washington County at the other agencies’ request. She said her agency “does not have and is not pursuing a ‘legislative carve out’ for any project.”

“My approach is to listen to partners’ concerns and explain our funding process,” she said in an email. “I have no role in deciding whether projects should receive funding as part of this process, and I do not advocate for individual projects. Characterizing these routine discussions and legitimate concerns as something improper fundamentally misrepresents their purpose and context.”

A spokesperson for Washington County’s housing authority told ProPublica that Bell did not make any commitment to alter the prioritization of Aloha 209th. Another Washington County spokesperson said the August meeting with Bell was mainly focused on the housing authority’s desire for “clearer criteria” for how projects on the state’s waitlist get funded.
A Metro spokesperson said the regional agency requested the September meeting with a goal “for the two agencies to strengthen our working relationship and coordination.”

“Metro does not, and did not, advocate for any specific project,” the spokesperson said. “We clearly indicated this at the meeting and in writing ahead of the meeting.” The agency has advocated for a group of remaining projects, including Aloha 209th, to get money so Metro can fulfill commitments made as part of its affordable housing bond, the spokesperson said.

Oregon’s Government Ethics Commission has until early December to complete its preliminary review of the complaint over Bell’s financial disclosure, which will help the agency decide whether to open a full investigation.
Bell said she will “continue to remain responsive to the Ethics Commission” as it completes its examination.

Kotek’s office, provided with a list of ProPublica’s latest findings, said in a statement that the governor “holds all agency leadership to consistent and high ethical standards” and that her office “is closely following” the ethics panel’s review.
The post Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing appeared first on ProPublica .

articles.title: Ancient Cahokia was transformed amid droughts and flooding – climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways
articles.author:
<name>AJ White, Assistant Professor of Anthropology, Indiana University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/aj-white-2768787"/>
paras: More than 800 years ago, a combination of environmental and societal challenges led some Mississippian people to leave Cahokia, a massive archaeological site that was once home to 20,000 people near modern-day St. Louis. Just south of Cahokia, another archaeological site is taking shape at Centreville, Illinois, as modern-day people abandon their homes in the face of 21st-century climate and cultural changes.
My anthropology colleague Sissel Schroeder and I studied both sites to learn how people react to climate change when it hits home.

During the 1960s and 1970s, economic downturns and the movement of white residents out of diversifying neighborhoods made Centreville into a majority-Black community that faced challenges such as mismanaged drainage infrastructure . Yet in interviews with a community group, residents reported that people had no major problems with living there until the floods came.

From the 1960s to the 2020s, average annual rainfall in the St. Louis region has increased by 10 inches (25 centimeters) to 44 inches (112 cm) a year. That has led to more frequent flooding , including in Centreville, where stormwater and sewage systems have not been significantly updated since they were built in the 1960s. The rains bring floods, which back up raw sewage into people’s kitchen sinks, and seep up through the ground, covering residents’ lawns as well as public streets and sidewalks.

Many people who can afford to move away from Centreville have done so, leaving a mostly older population and many abandoned homes . Essentially, a community is becoming an archaeological site before our eyes.

Nine hundred years ago, Cahokia occupied the same floodplain as Centreville does today. At its population peak around 1100 CE, over 100 burial, residential and ceremonial earthen mounds stretched from one end of the valley to the other, with its core centered on Monks Mound.

Monks Mound is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. It is 950 feet (290 meters) long and 775 feet (236 meters) wide, and its platform rises 100 feet (30 meters) above the floodplain. Decades of archaeological excavation show that surrounding Monks Mound are plazas that held great feasts and possibly sporting events – including chunkey, something like bocce ball with spears – timber monuments likely for ritually observing astronomical events, and other mounds containing elaborate burials .

Possibly up to 20,000 people lived at Cahokia at the start of the 12th century, but by the end of the century, the city had entered a population decline that continued for 200 years . Archaeologists have long debated the cause of Cahokia’s depopulation before European explorers and colonists arrived, putting forward a range of societal and environmental theories .

In other research, several colleagues and I previously found that Cahokia experienced several natural disasters during a warming period known as the Medieval Climatic Anomaly . In the second half of the 12th century, Cahokia experienced a large Mississippi River flood and drought conditions that stretched for several decades. Our study argued that the site’s depopulation was related to those climatic changes .

Climate change at Cahokia didn’t look like catastrophic scenes in movies like “The Day After Tomorrow .” There’s no evidence to suggest widespread destruction or death. Departures began at a time that coincided with climatic changes of the 12th century, but people continued to gradually leave the site through the 13th and 14th centuries.

As people left, life in Cahokia changed. After 1200 CE, archaeological evidence suggests Cahokians ceased or reduced communal feasting and mound building. They also contributed less to public granaries, moving agricultural surplus to private spaces. But it only became harder to live there for some people: Larger houses and status symbols became more prevalent, perhaps indicating a larger gap between the rich and poor.
To understand the relationship between social and environmental changes at Cahokia, I look at what is happening at Centreville in the 21st century.

People are not leaving all at once; instead, the accumulation of years of flooding-related failing infrastructure, repair costs and health problems have pushed some away from the community. Others have stayed, like resident William McNeal, who told a local news outlet, “ I’m not going to abandon my house . It’s all I got.”

Additionally, what’s happening in Centreville reveals that climate change is experienced unequally – some people are more affected than others. All of the St. Louis area has received increased rainfall and flooding in recent decades, but the residents of Centreville face some of the worst consequences because they live in a floodplain with outdated infrastructure.

At Cahokia, people would have also experienced the environmental events of the 12th century in different, unequal ways. Those with farms in the lower floodplain were most exposed to crop loss from flooding , but plots in the uplands were safer. During drought conditions, fields in well-drained soils likely retained less moisture and fared worse than plots with poorly drained soils.

People who lost crops may have struggled to contribute to communal feasts and shared food storage . I believe some may have become indebted to neighbors whose resources remained intact, while others may have decided to leave. Over time, these individual responses could have changed the relationships and inequalities that structured Cahokian society.
If that’s what happened, climate change did not cause a sudden and dramatic exodus from Cahokia. Instead, its uneven effects altered the social status quo; some benefited, some lost , and some left .

Today, some consequences of climate change can be major and immediate, such as sudden massive floods . But in communities like Centreville, the effects of repeated flooding accumulate over years, producing gradual societal changes that are harder to recognize than the aftermath of a sudden catastrophe.

Climate models are useful for estimating future conditions, but they reveal nothing about how people might experience or respond to those conditions. Events and people’s reactions may unfold quickly, even suddenly, or they may play out quietly over long periods of time.
Regardless, the result may be the stillness of an archaeological site.

articles.title: Sewing an infinity of phalluses – how Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama confronted the male-dominated art world by mocking it
articles.author:
<name>Midori Yamamura, Associate Professor of Art History, City University of New York</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/midori-yamamura-2761694"/>
paras: Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama’s installations are big, bold and controversial. From the time she burst upon the pop art scene in the 1960s until her death on Aug. 14, 2026, at the age of 97, she challenged the Western, male-dominated art world. She also upended assumptions about mental disorders, which many people have uncritically seen as the source of her creativity . Her phallic sculptures and confounding mirror rooms are still popular, and they defy artistic classifications.
Kusama’s resistance to categorization raises an intriguing question: What is her lasting effect on the art world?

Kusama took a major step into the global art scene after sending two canvases for display at Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum on Feb. 5, 1962. After that, she shifted her direction to avant-garde sculpture. She created Accumulation No. 1 , her first work in a series that employed sewn phallic protrusions. The series thrust her into New York City’s pop art scene and would lead to her fantastical Infinity Mirror Rooms installation.
A major retrospective of her work is on view at the Stedelijk Museum through Jan. 17, 2027.

The specter of her mental health issues, however, still undermines her art’s significance. Critics often link the repetition in her work to obsessive-compulsive disorder. But as an art historian who has studied Kusama extensively, I argue that she intentionally used compulsivity to examine gender issues in the art world. A close look at Accumulation No. 1 reveals how she pulled this off.

Kusama’s emphasis on gender came into focus when she arrived in the male-dominated New York art world . During the 1940s and 50s, while abstract expressionism reigned in New York, women in the scene were treated as wives and assistants.

Painter Grace Hartigan had to adopt the pseudonym “George” to gain recognition. By the 1960s, that was starting to change. Venezuelan sculptor Marisol Escobar’s May 1962 exhibition at the Stable Gallery bucked the trend of gender conformity by integrating self-portraits into her sculpture series.

Kusama’s Accumulation No. 1 emerged as New York artists were seeking to move beyond abstract expressionism . The gestural paintings of this art movement were what some critics saw as an existential struggle toward originality coded as masculine . Pop artists refused this model : They turned instead to ready-made objects and impersonal repetition, evoking factory production.

Kusama procured furniture and egg cartons for her Accumulation sculptures, as well as a wooden rowboat for another sculpture that became Aggregation One Thousand Boats Show . She decided to focus on sewing — an art rooted in her female Japanese education — and she ordered a sewing machine.

Kusama embraced femininity by using phalluses – a symbol of patriarchal authority – made from assorted fabrics sewn into tubular shapes, filled with cotton and painted white. She upholstered an armchair with these protrusions, colonizing an eerie domestic scene with phalluses made through a traditionally feminine craft.
In this way, she transformed furniture into a vessel of complex meaning, with gender as the key component to interpretation.

Art critics and scholars have often interpreted the time-consuming process of creating these phalluses as evidence of obsessive-compulsive neurosis . But this assumption overshadows Kusama’s careful planning and deliberate choices in her art. Intensive manual labor is a common component of Kusama’s work.

In 2008, filmmaker Heather Lenz interviewed Kusama’s friend Helen Yrissary, who helped sew the protrusions on the armchair. She noted that while there were always five assistants who crafted the phalluses, only Kusama herself secured them to the chair. In Accumulation No. 1 and Accumulation No. 2, obsession was more of a calculated aesthetic and conceptual choice than a compulsive action.

Kusama knew about obsessive-compulsive disorder and the anxiety it can cause. Drawing on Sigmund Freud’s psychoanalytical theories, she explained in her autobiography that she developed the phallic image while she was exploring “kyōfu” – fear, or feelings of the uncanny – in the Accumulation series. According to Freud, the potential for the uncanny is rooted in a child’s first awareness of the anatomical differences between the sexes. He postulated that female children are traumatized when they realize they lack a penis, creating what he called penis envy .
Kusama’s Accumulation series may have functioned as a satire of penis envy . And it may have led her to the idea of vanquishing men’s authoritative power.

In one of her self-portraits from 1966 , Kusama flaunted a phallic protrusion near her crotch. This gesture suggests that the protrusion might be her own penis, that she might be bisexual or that she might not fall under the category of “female.” Such efforts to redefine female sexuality inspired many female artists at the time. Toward the late 1960s, artist Louise Bourgeois , who admired Kusama’s work, created several sculptures, including Fillette (Little Girl) , that employed phallic shapes as commentary on psychological complexes and gender.

But when Kusama premiered Accumulation No. 1 and Accumulation No. 2, The New York Times gave her work only a brief mention . When, three months later, sculptor Claes Oldenburg showed his similarly sewn “metamorphic” sculptures, he received rave reviews in numerous art magazines, bringing him to the attention of the international art world. It was only much later in the 2010s, after Kusama gained global prominence, that Oldenburg admitted her influence on his work.

Kusama’s popularity today stems from works that are both visually expansive and socially subversive. Aggregation: One Thousand Boats Show was her first all-over exhibit – an exhibition in which a repeated motif covers the gallery’s four walls, drawing the audience into the work rather than asking them to view it as a separate object. On display at the Gertrude Stein Gallery from December 1963 to January 1964, it featured a sculpture of the phallus-embedded boat surrounded by its image repeating across the wall.

Although Kusama sought to subvert male authority, she appears nude in a photograph of the phallus boat installation , her back to the camera, trapped between the real and the illusory. Rowing the boat seems like the only way to escape the omnipresence of masculinity.
She seemed even more entrapped by patriarchal symbolism in her Infinity Mirror Room — Phalli’s Field, where she lays among an array of phalluses covered in red polka dots.

In 1966, Kusama found a way to break away from male domination through her “ Peep Show ” at the Castellane Gallery in New York. In it, she reduced the towering phallus to a small dot of light. It was her first work of psychedelic art , a category the curator Christoph Grunenberg characterized as both “ artistic experiment and dissenting politics .”

Incorporating Beatles music, flickering strobe lights and mirror reflections, “Peep Show” was intended to produce effects similar to those of psychoactive drugs such as mescaline, psilocybin and LSD, liberating users from established social norms and opening the possibility of alternative values. The exhibit, later known as “ Love Forever ,” also aimed to alter perception by inducing synesthesia — a neurological state in which stimulating one sensory-cognitive pathway triggers involuntary experiences in another.

Kusama remembered attending a lecture by Timothy Leary , a former Harvard University psychology professor and psychedelics advocate, at the Village Theater in New York, a hub of psychedelic culture. In 1968, she collaborated with light artist Joshua White on Self-Obliteration , a fusion of sound, lights and images that Leary claimed “would demonstrate what an LSD session is like.”

Kusama’s ability to transform any neurosis she may have had into liberation began with Accumulation No. 1 and continued through Fireflies on the Water (2002), Soul Under the Moon (2002), Infinity Mirror Room—Aftermath of Obliteration of Eternity (2009) and Infinity Mirrored Room—The Souls of Millions of Light Years Away (2013). The ethereal visions embodied in her psychedelic mirror rooms stand in for the mind-altering drugs that release people from the rationality of society and fuel the desire to change.

Through Kusama’s Accumulation and Infinity Mirror Room series, I argue that she turned the human body into what philosopher Herbert Marcuse described as “ an instrument of pleasure .” By making the body an instrument of pleasure rather than labor, Kusama subverted the age-old patriarchal order.
Midori Yamamura received funding from the Smithsonian American Art Museum's Terra Foundation for her research on Yayoi Kusama.

articles.title: Georgians mark 2 years of pro-EU demonstrations – defying campaign to wear protesters down
articles.author:
<name>Regina Smyth, Professor of Political Science, Indiana University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/regina-smyth-456488"/>
paras: For months on end, Georgians have braved the elements and long odds to protest their government’s suspension of the former Soviet country’s bid to join the European Union. On Nov. 28, 2026, those pro-democracy campaigners will mark a milestone – two years of sustained, if declining, protest.

Hailed as a beacon of democracy following its independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, Georgia has of late been increasingly held up as an example of democratic backsliding : the slow, persistent erosion of democratic institutions. Indeed, the 2025 Economist Democracy Index — an annual benchmark of global democratic health — found that Georgia had fallen 20 places on the list since 2017.

The formal hallmarks of democratic systems remain visible: Elections are held, parliaments vote and political parties organize. At the same time, democratic institutions are compromised by political leaders, parties, police, courts and legislators – who use their resources to stifle dissent and compromise democratic institutions .

These leaders commonly target electoral fairness without committing blatant fraud. For example, public sector workers such as teachers are threatened with job loss if they do not vote for the government, or local governments are rewarded for producing votes during elections. Critics allege that biased laws and politicized court cases eliminate independent media and jail opposition leaders.

Backsliding governments also use disinformation and rhetoric to create confusion and fear. Using these tactics, critics allege, the ruling populist right, pro-Russian Georgian Dream government continues to undermine the fragile democracy. With many feeling unable to fight back through elections and parliamentary debates, Georgians have taken to the streets .

I am a member of a research project that explores how national protests in countries with fragile democratic institutions create legacies that can influence politics over the long term. In Georgia, that work is based on interviews with leaders from across civic and political life. These interviews point to a widespread view that the government is actively attempting to erode protest just as critics of the government feel it has eroded institutions. So far, the government has not crushed the movement with a campaign of lethal force. Rather, it has tried to use lower-level, but sustained, suppression tactics in hopes of inducing burnout in the opposition and getting civil society to disengage .

In Georgia, the roots of protest are deep in the struggle for independence from the Soviet Union and the influence of Russia under the leadership of Vladimir Putin. In 2003, Georgians launched the Rose Revolution – the first in a series of actions across the former Soviet states called the Color Revolutions – to support democracy and autonomy from the Russian Federation.

The Georgian Dream emerged as a socially conservative opposition party in 2012 under the leadership of the billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili and won a majority of seats in parliamentary elections. Many analysts at the time saw the party as a new chance to consolidate democracy. Yet unable to provide economic gains , the party instead embarked on a platform consistent with pro-Russian security policies, which critics allege were rife with political manipulation, and false rhetoric that undermined democracy. In 2019 , Georgians took to the streets to contest failed electoral reforms and growing Russian influence through Ivanishvili’s governance.

By 2023, tens of thousands of Georgians filled Rustaveli Avenue in the capital of Tbilisi to oppose a law designed to shutter civic organizations and independent media. The so-called Russia Law borrowed heavily from the Kremlin’s tactics to eliminate opposition to the Putin government in Russia. Many Georgians understood the law as an attack on democracy and celebrated when the ruling party, Georgian Dream, withdrew its bill .

A year later, as new elections approached, the party reintroduced the law, provoking renewed protest. This time it passed. A few months later, preelection polls showed the opposition parties leading, but expectations of victory evaporated when Georgia Dream secured 54% of vote – an outcome that critics raised as a possible indicator of electoral manipulation .

Then, on Nov. 28, 2024, the new government put Georgia’s European Union bid on hold until 2028. Many Georgians have long seen EU membership as a path forward to economic growth and democratic protections . In light of Russia’s 2008 occupation of Georgian territory and 2022 full-scale war in Ukraine, Georgians also perceived EU membership as a bulwark against Russian intervention.

Fueled by feelings of betrayal over the reversal on EU membership, crowds poured back onto Rustaveli Avenue, reaching a peak of 170,000-200,000 protesters. Several hundred activists have returned every day since.

Over the course of two years, Georgian protesters have faced chronic and unpredictable violence rather than a decisive crackdown. By Amnesty International’s count , thousands have been arrested, hundreds beaten in the streets or abused in custody, and more than 150 imprisoned after politically motivated trials.

In general, however, the Georgian government’s tactic for countering the protest movement has been to avoid mass violence in lieu of targeted attacks on protest leaders and subtler means to discourage new activists. Fines for protest rose tenfold between 2024 and 2026 to double the average Georgian’s monthly income, leading Amnesty International to conclude that Georgia’s courts have become tools for “financially exhausting protesters.” Meanwhile, repeat offenses for participating in a demonstration have become crimes.

These actions have steadily increased the costs of protesting, driving activists from the streets due to a multitude of reasons related to risk, personal safety and fear. In our research, we protect the people we interviewed from state retaliation by making them anonymous.
The effects of these costs are clear in their statements.
“We don’t say it openly,” an investigative journalist and editor told us. “But the truth is, we were exhausted, depleted — and that’s the state we were in when the election campaign started.”

Another pro-European student movement member said, “Human resources are exhausted. You can’t expect 300,000 or 100,000 or even 20,000 people to march from Ilia University to Parliament every single day for 200 or 300 days straight. People have jobs, lives, personal struggles, and you can’t ask them to drop everything every day.”

Overall, our interviews with a variety of civil society leaders and protest supporters found that exhaustion was widespread and that a declining amount of people had the physical, financial or emotional capacity to stand every day.

Still, leaders remain hopeful that the nightly protests will provide a platform for renewed activism when the next opportunity for challenging the government presents itself. As the same pro-European student movement member argued: “I believe that will change. Let’s say Georgians are just on a kind of protest vacation. I hope we’ll be back out there again, all together, very soon.”

For now, there exists an effective stalemate between the protest movement and the government. The movement endures but has not broken through, and I believe the government cannot crush it because it fears the student leader is right — and the protest vacation might end.
For a generation of Georgians invested in building democracy, the past two years have shown how quickly democratic gains can be undone.

Still, as the anniversary of nightly protests approaches, many Georgians point to Serbia, where student protesters also took the streets in November 2024 and forced an early election on Oct. 25, 2026. The same Serbian students formed an opposition bloc that won a parliamentary majority that unseated an entrenched and increasingly autocratic leader .
Georgian Dream understands this threat and has proposed a ban on opposition parties, closing the route that Serbia’s students used.

Yet a policy of attrition has its risk, as ruling in that manner can further erode legitimacy and incur the high costs of keeping elites loyal. In the meantime, the protests continue, which could yet provide oxygen for renewed opposition when a new crisis arises.
Tinatin Genebashvili, a U.S.-based Georgian researcher and founder of Research Hub, contributed to this article.

articles.title: Columbia is keeping its gates closed, raising the question of what universities owe their neighborhoods
articles.author:
<name>Austin Sarat, William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science, Amherst College</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/austin-sarat-174772"/>
paras: The Gaza war protests that overtook some colleges and universities in 2023 and 2024 have long dispersed – but one very clear remnant of the demonstrations remains at Columbia University’s Morningside Heights campus in New York City: a closed campus.

Columbia’s administration first shut the gates in April 2024, following pro-Palestinian rights protests and waves of police arrests . New York City politicians said that these disruptions were fueled by “outside agitators.”
Now, only students, faculty, staff and alumni with a school ID are able to enter Columbia’s quad.

Some of Columbia’s neighbors sued the university in January 2025, saying that the closure created a “six-block barrier between Broadway and Amsterdam Avenue from West 120th to West 114th Street” and violated the Americans with Disabilities Act and Rehabilitation Act .

A New York Supreme Court judge in Manhattan dismissed their suit on Nov. 10, 2026, saying that “even if Columbia previously granted unrestricted public access to College Walk, as it remained their private property, nothing prevented them from restricting access at any time.” The plaintiffs quickly appealed the decision .
Columbia has maintained that safety concerns meant it needed to close its gates, and that the campus is private property.

Nonetheless, in the past, Columbia allowed neighbors to cross the campus as a scenic shortcut through the neighborhood. Nearby nursery schools used the campus green as a place for children to explore and play.

As a college professor of law and political science, and an elected official in the western Massachusetts town where I teach , the Columbia campus controversy feels familiar. These “town-and-gown” disputes have, from time to time, raised questions about what universities owe the community beyond their gates.

From at least the 1950s until 2024, Columbia had an open campus policy. In 1953, New York City approved closing the campus’s central West 116th Street stretch to cars, with the understanding that pedestrians would be able to walk across the campus.

The recent closure stirred up tensions between the school and its neighbors. But such strains are as old as universities themselves. Some commentators suggest that conflict between universities and their surrounding communities can be traced back to medieval Europe.

“The early universities in cities such as Bologna and Paris took a very different form to the institutions we know today. They were loose communities of masters and scholars who lived amongst the people of the town,” the education historian Harley Richardson wrote in 2020 .

Townspeople often resented those scholars and students because “They couldn’t understand the scholarly Latin spoken by the students” or whether “the long gowns they wore” were “intended to convey a superior social status,” Richardson wrote.

One of the most notorious town-gown incidents that turned violent occurred in Oxford, England, in February 1354 on so-called St. Scholastica Day, honoring an Italian saint who founded the order of the Benedictine nuns .

Trouble began in a local tavern when some students complained loudly and aggressively about the poor quality of the wine they were served. Things escalated when the tavern-keeper, who was also the mayor of Oxford, responded with insults. A fight broke out and drew in a large number of townspeople and students who rushed to the scene. It took the intervention of the king to restore order.
Conflicts between universities and their local towns or cities have also been very much a part of the story of higher education in the United States.
Most often these disputes have focused on issues like where a university should build a dormitory or whether it should pay fees to the city where it is located.
And as in England, these conflicts have occasionally turned violent.
One such incident happened in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1806, when riots broke out between Yale University students and locals who were on their way to church.
What, if anything, do universities owe their communities ?

The popular phrase “ the ivory tower ” captures one vision of a university. It suggests that universities serve society by being left alone to conduct research and educate students, disengaged from the larger community’s immediate concerns. In this view, people outside of universities benefit indirectly from the inventions and innovations that universities produce, as well as from the jobs they create.

Another vision, which came to prominence in the 1960s, called on universities to be good citizens of their surrounding communities. This view urged university leaders to invest in their neighborhoods.

Colby College, in Waterville, Maine, exemplifies this approach . It has spent US$265 million on construction and other investment projects over the past several years , with an eye on revitalizing its struggling downtown district .

Others schools, including the University of Notre Dame , the University of Pennsylvania , the University of Southern California and the University of California, San Francisco , have invested substantial amounts of money in developing their towns and cities and supporting neighbors. Trinity College in Hartford, Connecticut, for example, announced in September 2026 that it would pay for the full tuition , housing and meals for local residents who are admitted as students.

Some universities have been sending students out into the communities around them as one way to support their city. For example, Columbia Journalism School students are often tasked with developing a reporting project in a particular New York City neighborhood.
And some leaders in higher education now talk openly about orienting their schools toward the promotion of the greater good.
A university investing in its surrounding community does not guarantee the end of tensions, which to me seem an inevitable part of the higher education landscape.
But when universities show their communities that civic responsibility is core to their mission, they build goodwill and offer a way of bridging divides when conflicts occur.

I don’t know how the Columbia campus dispute will resolve. But as newly elected New York State Assemblyman Eli Northrop observed : “Columbia is successful when Morningside Heights is successful and when the relationship between the neighborhood and the university is good.”

articles.title: Immersive shopping has survived the demise of the metaverse – but its appeal depends on how it’s designed and who is using it
articles.author:
<name>Hyejune Park, Associate Professor, Oklahoma State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/hyejune-park-1168814"/>
paras: In 2021 and 2022, major retailers and fashion brands were racing into the metaverse , opening virtual stores, creating digital products and inviting consumers to explore branded worlds through avatars. Much of that excitement has since faded. But the technologies behind those experiments are far from disappearing .

Today, shoppers can try on clothes virtually, see how furniture would look in their homes and explore branded worlds on gaming platforms. Rather than building entirely new virtual universes, retailers are finding ways to integrate immersive technologies into familiar shopping experiences.

A 2025 global survey found that 53% of surveyed retail professionals focused on virtual fitting rooms , while 46% said they were building augmented reality and virtual reality experiences. On the consumer side, a 2024 survey of more than 2,200 U.S. shoppers found that 49% of respondents would buy more clothing if a great virtual try-on experience were available. Meanwhile, a separate survey found that only 4.5% of U.S. digital shoppers regularly used these technologies for shopping.
Immersive technologies continue to attract interest, but their regular use in online shopping remains limited. So what makes an immersive shopping experience worth using?

I’m a scholar of retail and consumer sciences who studies consumers’ interactions with technology in the retail environment. My research suggests that the value of immersive retail isn’t simply about how advanced or realistic the technology is. It’s about how the experience is designed, how it addresses consumers’ needs and how it helps them connect with products and brands.

Imagine shopping for a pair of sunglasses online. You like the style, but you’re not sure how they would look on you. Amazon allows shoppers to try on certain shoes and eyewear virtually using their smartphones. IKEA applies a similar concept to home furnishings through IKEA Kreativ, which allows customers to digitally remove existing furniture from their rooms and experiment with new arrangements.
These experiences address a fundamental limitation of online shopping: the gap between seeing a product on a screen and imagining how it would look on you or in your own space.

My colleagues and I found that the experience of virtually trying on clothes can be particularly helpful for shoppers who struggle to imagine how clothing would look on them. By making it easier to visualize themselves wearing a product, the technology can help them feel more comfortable with their purchase decisions. In other words, the value of immersive technology may lie less in creating a sense of novelty than in helping consumers overcome the limitations of conventional online shopping.

As artificial intelligence advances, so-called virtual try-on experiences are becoming increasingly personalized. Shoppers can now see clothing on digital representations of themselves rather than relying solely on images of fashion models. It might seem intuitive that the more closely a virtual model resembles a shopper, the better the experience. But our research suggests otherwise .

In two experiments, we found that consumers’ responses to personalized avatars depend on what psychologists call “ assessment orientation ,” or the tendency to critically evaluate and compare options before making a decision. This mindset of carefully thinking through a decision can also shift depending on the shopping situation, such as choosing an outfit for a job interview versus casually browsing for fun.

Shoppers with a stronger evaluative mindset, whether due to their personal tendencies or the shopping situation, felt a stronger sense that they were the model and expressed greater intentions to buy when using personalized 3D avatars than when viewing conventional model images. Interestingly, the opposite pattern emerged among shoppers who are less inclined to mull over options.

The implication is that the same technology can offer different value to different consumers. A highly personalized experience may be particularly useful to someone who wants to thoroughly evaluate a product, but it isn’t necessarily better for everyone or every shopping situation.
Immersive technologies can also offer value beyond helping consumers decide what to buy.

Walmart, for example, has created branded experiences on Roblox , where users can explore virtual spaces, play games and discover digital products. These experiences offer retailers a new way to connect with younger consumers and build brand engagement through entertainment rather than traditional advertising. Its Walmart Discovered Roblox gaming environment has attracted nearly 40 million visits as of May 2026.

My research on branded virtual worlds suggests that simply creating a virtual space isn’t enough to engage consumers. What matters is how brands bring these spaces to life through storytelling and social experiences that help consumers feel more connected to the brand. The value of these environments lies less in their 3D graphics than in the opportunities they create for consumers to participate, interact and become part of a brand’s story.

Advances in AI will likely open up even more possibilities for immersive online shopping, from more realistic virtual try-on to interactive environments that adapt to individual preferences. But making an experience more technologically sophisticated doesn’t automatically make it more valuable.

Whether a retailer’s goal is to help shoppers visualize products, make more informed decisions or build connections with brands, they are more likely to be successful if they design experiences around consumers rather than around the capabilities of the technology.

articles.title: Why expect holiday traditions to stay the same, even as life continually changes?
articles.author:
<name>Lee Ann Rawlins Williams, Clinical Assistant Professor of Education, Health and Behavior Studies, University of North Dakota</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/lee-ann-rawlins-williams-1486589"/>
paras: There’s something about the holiday season that makes people notice the passage of time. As you unpack treasured decorations, prepare family recipes and listen to familiar holiday songs, you’re reminded not only of celebrations from years past but also of different times in your life.

With each passing year, children grow older, families welcome new members, relationships change, and some of those you once celebrated with are no longer here. But people often approach the holidays hoping to experience them just as they once did.

As someone who studies life transitions , I’m particularly interested in why people expect traditional holiday celebrations to remain the same when so much else in life has changed. I suggest thinking of holiday memories not as a blueprint for recreating the past but as a way to understand what makes these times meaningful to you, and how you might carry that meaning into the present.

Research on family rituals suggests that traditions contribute to a sense of identity and belonging by connecting you to the people, experiences and shared values that have shaped your life. In fact, research focused on holiday rituals has found that participating in traditions such as preparing grandmother’s chocolate fudge or watching favorite seasonal movies is associated with greater feelings of closeness and enjoyment during celebrations.

You may not recognize how tightly some holiday traditions are tied to certain stages of your life. Parents who once looked forward to Christmas morning with young children may now find themselves coordinating celebrations around the schedules of adult children and their families and in-laws. Someone who has hosted holiday gatherings for decades may find themselves adjusting to being a guest rather than orchestrating the festivities.
Although these kinds of changes are a natural part of life, they can bring a mix of emotions. You can welcome new experiences while still missing aspects of an earlier time.
During these periods of transition, the memories associated with holiday traditions may become especially meaningful, offering a connection to the past as you adjust to the present.

If you find yourself missing the holidays of years past, you may be longing not for the celebration itself but for a particular era. Memories of former times can bring comfort, but they can also evoke feelings of grief, loneliness or sadness , particularly if you’re navigating changes you didn’t anticipate or would not have chosen, such as illness, injury, unemployment or relationship breakdown.
People may be more inclined to experience nostalgia, a sentimental longing for the past , during periods of transition , when familiar aspects of life are changing.
While nostalgia is sometimes viewed negatively, as dwelling on past experiences, research suggests it can be a valuable resource when navigating life changes, especially for younger generations .

For instance, nostalgia can actually strengthen social connections and contribute to a sense of meaning. Recalling cherished memories can remind you you’re part of a broader life story, which can enhance feelings of connection, personal value and purpose.
Nostalgia can also help people make sense of the different chapters of life, allowing them to maintain a sense of who they are even as circumstances change.

Memories, then, can be more than reminders of what once was. They can help you recognize what you value and inform how you experience the present. While nostalgia may not ease the pain associated with challenges such as major health changes, evolving caregiving responsibilities or military deployment, it can serve as a bridge between the past and the present.

Throughout life, people adjust routines, responsibilities and expectations to accommodate new circumstances. Yet when it comes to the holidays, they may be reluctant to make those same adjustments. Is it still Thanksgiving if the table doesn’t feature the cranberry sauce made with your family’s traditional recipe? Can it feel like Christmas if there’s no tree decorated with your family’s sentimental ornaments?

This reluctance to let holiday observances evolve may be influenced, in part, by how people remember previous celebrations. Negative emotions associated with past experiences tend to fade more quickly than positive ones . You may remember the warmth of gathering around a holiday table but less readily recall the stress or challenges that accompanied it.

When expectations no longer reflect the realities of your life, you may feel disappointed or place pressure on yourself or others to live up to those old memories. Even a cherished tradition can become a source of stress when you feel obligated to maintain it in the same way year after year.

As you navigate life’s transitions, it may be helpful to reflect on what you cherish most about your holiday traditions. Is it the way you have always celebrated? Or is it the feelings of comfort and belonging that you associate with those celebrations?
Research suggests that reflecting on the past can inspire people to seek meaningful connections and experiences in the present .

Of course, adjusting to change is not always easy, and for some, the holidays can be particularly hard . Adapting does not mean abandoning cherished traditions, directly replacing what has been lost, or feeling pressured to create new memories. It may simply mean accepting that the holidays will feel different and allowing yourself the time and space to adjust.

In the desire to recreate what once was, many people may overlook the moments that could become cherished memories in the years ahead. Savor the memories of holidays past without expecting them to define how you experience the holidays today. Celebrations don’t need to remain the same to remain meaningful.

articles.title: More art, less artificial: Seattle Art Museum billboards troll tech ads and tell people to look up
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: A billboard taking a swipe at Anthropic’s Claude might sound like the work of a rival AI company. This one is from the Seattle Art Museum .

“The only Claude you need is Monet,” the sign reads. It’s part of the latest wave of messages in SAM’s “Dear Seattle” campaign, which has spent the fall urging people to look up from their screens and see something in person.

Earlier billboards around the city told passersby to “come stare at something that isn’t your inbox” and noted that “even the algorithm thinks you should get out more.” The final batch pushes the AI jokes further, including one asking for “a little more art and a little less artificial” and another promising, “Your phone doesn’t have to know.”
Tech billboards are a fixture in the San Francisco Bay Area, where AI startups cover Highway 101 and city streets with ads that often mean little to anyone outside the industry.

They’re less common around Seattle. Anthropic put up a big orange Claude billboard over Aurora Avenue in 2024, and this spring Bellevue startup Summation put one up along SR 520 because “startup energy should be more visible around here,” its CEO told GeekWire.

“In a city where so much of our lives happens on screens, we’re making a playful case for the things you can only experience in person,” Kat Bryant Flaherty, SAM’s director of communications, said in a statement. She listed “the scale and texture of an artwork, a film with a room full of strangers, making something with your hands, or catching up with a friend over a meal.”

The campaign is tied to changes at the downtown museum itself, where SAM is adding more public space and more reasons to linger, including hands-on art making and music in the Studio at SAM and the newly opened Bar Dojo restaurant.
The campaign runs through the end of the year, with more than 200 ads across the region — more than 20 billboards plus spots on light rail and digital kiosks.
SAM’s campaign is about the same size as the one Bellevue startup Statsig ran in the Bay Area in 2024, with more than 200 billboards and transit posters, but pointed in the opposite direction.

SAM is offering buy-one-get-one-free tickets in December with the code “LOVESAM,” good at both the downtown museum and the Seattle Asian Art Museum in Volunteer Park, to encourage people to visit together.
“We’re hoping to grab attention, spark curiosity, and remind Seattle that there’s a lot happening at SAM worth leaving the house for,” Flaherty said.

articles.title: Delridge Station bus loop
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: Earlier this year Sound Transit provided a simplified design for the Delridge Link Station. If the West Seattle Link Extension gets built, Ross pointed out how RapidRide H buses will need to detour to serve the station. That would eliminate any travel time advantages gained by running on rails even if bus and trains would align their departure time perfectly. Instead of such detour, what about if the buses would just stop on Delridge Way and riders could take an overpass to the platform going north? It’s similar to RapidRide A buses stopping on International Blvd and riders taking an overpass to reach the airport station.
As most riders are expected to reach the station by bus, in particular RapidRide H, the transfer experience will be critical.

Early on Sound Transit had considered various designs for the Delridge Link station. Before settling on the location in front of the steel plant, one such design had been right above and along Delridge Way. Busses would have stopped right underneath, and riders could have just taken an escalator up to the departing platform. That would have provided a great transfer experience. With the current alignment and station location, designing a great transfer experience is more complicated. For southbound buses, Sound Transit plans a station along Delridge Way. For northbound buses, Sound Transit proposes that the buses detour from the red bus lane on the right to take a left turn into SW Andover St and a right turn into the station (see blue line on map below). But that also means buses have to pull out of the station and turn left again to get back to Delridge Way. Along the way they may need to navigate around the large trucks serving the steel plant. While riders get dropped off right under the Link platform, the various turns each bus has to navigate may add several minutes to the transfer.

If Sound Transit would instead add a northbound bus stop along Delridge Way across from the southbound bus stop and an overpass connecting to the northbound Link platform (see red lines on map), then riders could arrive quite quickly. (Southbound riders would need to take the escalator/elevator down and up again)

Sound Transit already plans a staircase on the NE corner of the station. Instead, they could build a staircase on the east side of Delridge Way and connect it with an overpass to the northbound platform. This would be similar to the way buses stop along the International Blvd to reach the airport station.

This would free up bus bays on the west side of the station. That space could be used as pickup/drop off and paratransit stop which may eliminate the need for the south car/van loop. That may allow larger housing developments on the south corner.

I am also concerned that the station entrance is quite a bit lower than Delridge Way. That may create some issues for riders who want to walk on the ground between buses along Delridge and the station. I really liked the plaza of the prior station design which allowed access to a mezzanine but understand that it adds cost. It would be great if the housing development could connect at least to the south staircases and elevators midway. If Sound Transit could add a small mezzanine under the tracks connecting the northbound and southbound southern staircases, it would help with at-grade walking to Delridge (and also switching platforms).

I still don’t think a Link extension to West Seattle is a good choice as buses could just drop riders off at SODO, but if we proceed with the plan, let’s at least optimize the existing design to improve the transfer experience as much as possible.

articles.title: Sound Transit Inches Forward Station Activation and Retail Plan
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: In leading transit systems around the world, shops and cafes are often integrated into the fabric of stations, with busier hubs even melding into full-scale shopping malls. That's decidedly not the case for the retail-scarce Sound Transit network or for most other agencies across the Seattle metropolitan area.

However, as Sound Transit has grown into the busiest light rail system in the United States, boasting more than 160,000 daily riders, policymakers are beginning to ask if it's time to change that. Sound Transit has implemented a few pilot programs, but a broader activation strategy could be on the horizon, potentially building out retail and community programming on a larger scale.

"Much of the work is still in early testing and pilot stages, but we are refining proof of concepts, and we do have an eye for wider expansions," Marie Olson, Sound Transit's executive director of rider experience and operations, told agency board members during a November 5 meeting.

Most of Sound Transit's early efforts at retail installations are located outside of Seattle, although Seattle (which is home to a majority of the region's light rail ridership ) has seen a few temporary markets and festivals near its stations.

Early efforts at creating permanent retail at Seattle stations have failed to take root. One enterprising vendor pushed to open up a coffee cart at Capitol Hill Station, but health code hurdles and general bureaucratic morass forced them to close up shop, as The Urbanist reported in June. Capitol Hill remains one of Sound Transit's busiest stations, so the opportunity remains once startup hurdles are cleared.

In 2022, Sound Transit welcomed a coffee shop before the neighboring Redmond Technology Station had even opened to light rail riders. At a presentation to the Rider Experience and Operations (REO) Committee on November 5, Marshall Foster, chief planning and development officer for Sound Transit, christened the project a success, pointing out that the Microsoft campus provides a built-in audience for the Dote coffee bar.

"That's your more traditional, built-out brick-and-mortar retail space," Foster said of Redmond's Dote bar. "I think we learned there that the power of having a built-in daily audience and market for retail is critical."

While Microsoft's Redmond HQ campus touts a headcount above 50,000, the light rail station next door is posting more modest figures, with just over 1,000 daily boardings. That's about a quarter of the boardings typically seen at the median 1 Line station, suggesting ample retail opportunities across the system. The modest ridership so far also hints that a good chunk of customers are visiting the coffee bar without riding light rail before or after.

In 2023, the agency opened The Roadhouse in Angle Lake, serving as a community performance space. That endeavor followed a failed attempt to establish a more retail-focused concept in the space, illustrating the value of tailoring a storefront to local needs and demand.
In 2025, a coffee shop opened at Lynnwood Station, and a hotdog stand recently set up shop at Federal Way.

"At Lynnwood City Center Station, we had a vacant space, which was purpose-built for a cafe-style vending, and we worked closely with Lynnwood and Snohomish Chambers [of Commerce]," Olson said. "We spread the word out to get solicitations. We also worked with the City of Lynnwood to get that word out. Caffe Ciao is in there now. They opened in the summer of 2025. Today they operate seven days a week, Monday through Friday, 5 am to 5 pm and Saturday and Sunday, 8 am to 3 pm. And they just renewed their lease for another two years."
Olson noted that Federal Way's hot dog stand is on a seven-month trial run.

"Our newest vendor [...] is Whatzz Up Dogg," Olson said. "[It] just opened this summer at Federal Way Downtown Station Plaza, and it's got a seven-month trial. It's a great spot, and it really brings that station to life if you've been out there."

Tacoma Councilmember Kristina Walker, who chairs the REO committee, agreed with Olson, saying the hot dog vendor "is the nicest, friendliest, most welcoming person ever, and he really has changed the energy at that station, I love it. So more of that. He's doing a great job."
Systemwide, riders have expressed strong interest in station retail, according to agency surveys.
"We did some survey work of our riders," Foster said. "We found that a little over 60% strongly wanted to see us bring more retail experiences into the station environment as part of their commute."
Sound Transit is looking at meeting that demand, where possible.

The next round of vending rollouts aim to put Seattle on the map, targeting the busiest station in the light rail system, Westlake, and the highest performing Eastside station, Bellevue Downtown. Westlake averages about 17,000 daily boardings, while Bellevue Downtown attracts around 2,500.

"Other pilots in the works include mobile coffee carts at Westlake mezzanine," Olson said. "We're also in the final stages of permitting a few beverage carts in the Bellevue Downtown Station. We're also scoping potential locations for vending machines at some stations. Initially, the three Federal Way Extension stations have good potential."

Westlake used to feature direct access to Nordstrom's department store from the mezzanine level, but that door has since been closed, with security cited as the reason. There is still a connection to Westlake Mall.

While the agency has been gradually rolling out pilot projects, Sound Transit has also been refining its broader vision for station activation. Foster pointed to hosting the FIFA World Cup and expanding the 2 Line across Lake Washington as watershed moments that pushed the agency to zoom out and look bigger picture about its longer term goals around retail and activation.

Earlier this year, as part of World Cup operations, Sound Transit set up an information booth in the former bus pass kiosk at Westlake, which had been turned into a security booth. Since then, the agency has kept the kiosk open.

"So, this is our strategic vision for station activation: We're striving to make each station reflective of the community in which it sits," Olson said. "Station activation will transform waiting and transitional spaces into engaging, welcoming, and community-centered environments that improve passenger experience."
The visioning work identified four pillars to station activation.

"Sound Transit is organizing station activations within four pillars that activate, engage, partner, and manage," Olson said. "Coffee carts, beverage vendors, farmers markets, food carts, pop-up retail, those will all be defined as 'activate' with an outcome of increased customer satisfaction and passenger comfort."
Sound Transit hosted 22 farmers markets this year at Angle Lake Station, Olson noted, with the help of African Community Housing and Development Ground, which organized the markets.

"Sound Transit is seeking an outcome of stronger emotional connection for passengers with their transit experience," Olson said. "Think live music, local artist features, arts and crafts, cultural celebrations. Sound Transit plans to continue to partner with local businesses and community organizations and artists."

The agency's "partner" pillar simply denotes an intent to increase partnerships with local businesses and community organizations and artists. Manage, meanwhile, was focused on crowd management during high-ridership events.

"The FIFA World Cup was held this summer. Sound Transit worked with over a dozen vendors to create programming at numerous stations downtown and across the system," Olson said. "Memorably, one of the most popular performances was the group that dressed up as astronauts and engage the crowds waiting to board the trains at International District Chinatown stations. These activities help create a festive atmosphere. They helped the crowd's spirits stay high, even when they were facing the long boarding times – great examples of implementing how we managed as a pillar of activation, integrating activities at stations to help manage the crowds."

Sound Transit has also advanced similar plans at Sounder stations and is considering Tacoma T Line streetcar stations. On the Sounder S Line, Auburn and Kent have retail as part of transit-oriented development projects. The staff presentation called out the five following early activation projects:

Through the first phase of study, Sound Transit also improved mapping of station areas, with an eye toward making it easier to throw events, such as farmers markets or festivals on the premises. For example, staff slides featured a Lynnwood City Center Station map that called areas that would require fire marshal approval to stage for events, while recommending locations for a main stage, tents, portable restrooms, food trucks, and additional food services.

Based on its initial research, Sound Transit appears to be gravitating toward outsourcing the work of overseeing and designing the retail program to third-party contractors – which is a well-established pattern for the agency, with outside vendors also performing core functions like security, transit engineering, marketing, etc.

"One of the critical things is what is our management model?" Foster said. "Is this something Sound Transit manages itself like we do our system, or do we bring in industry expertise? In this case, I think we're leaning, based on the experience of our team and talking with other systems across the country, that we should potentially bring in some third-party partners who are experts in retail to help manage this component of our system."

Part of the obstacle to rolling out food service enterprises are health code requirements for bathrooms and sinks and other utilities and infrastructure that many stations lack, at least in the public portion of the station.

"Whether it's utilities or access to restrooms, the very specific requirements of Seattle King County Public Health around that and other public health agencies, that's critical work that we'll be doing as part of that next phase," Foster said.
Foster expects to return to share findings with the board in 2027.

While the first two phases of Sound Transit's expansions have been completed with very few retail venues included in stations and limited opportunities to easily add them after the fact, Sound Transit 3 (ST3) projects are still in fairly early phases of design and present opportunities for retail and community spaces to be incorporated from the jump. Of course, the catch is that ST3 projects are already under severe budgetary strain and could face pressure to avoid costs seen as tertiary or optional in order to ensure the projects make it across the finish line.

On the other hand, some have argued that rider comfort and basic amenities that improve it should not be treated as expendable and easily jettisoned. Retrofitting those amenities later could end up being more expensive in the long-run with less optimal outcomes possible when not designing stations for activation from the beginning.

King County Councilmember Claudia Balducci said that work to retrofit retail facilities into existing stations could in turn expand rider amenities for non-patrons by providing public bathrooms at more stations. Conversely, designing stations to have public bathrooms from day one is good for the daily rider experience, beyond just retail and festival opportunities.

"I just want to add my voice to anything we can do to make the station areas more comfortable for our riders," Balducci said. "As we do longer term retail leases, particularly, I'm very supportive of us working with our partners to open those bathrooms to riders that exist for the purposes of whatever retail they may be doing."

articles.title: Seattle Real Time Crime Center video captures Capitol Hill armed carjacking attempt but suspects elude police
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: It will be a quieter holiday week on CHS but we’re still working. See something others should know about? Email CHS or call/txt (206) 399-5959 . You can view recent CHS 911 coverage here. Hear sirens and wondering what’s going on? Check out reports from @jseattle or join and check in with neighbors in the CHS Facebook Group .

Surveillance cameras part of Seattle’s Real Time Crime Center captured video of an armed attempted carjacking that ended on Capitol Hill early Saturday morning but the suspects were able to elude officers following a brief I-5 pursuit, according to the Seattle Police Department .

The incident unfolded around 12:22 AM when a frantic driver sped up to officers patrolling the nightlife district near the 1000 block of E Pike. The victim reported that a Dodge SUV carrying four men had been chasing him, and that an occupant of the SUV armed with a firearm exited the vehicle at one point and tried to enter his car before he managed to flee.
Using the city’s camera network, police say the Real Time Crime Center located video evidence showing the victim’s account of the chase and armed confrontation.

Using the suspect vehicle’s description, officers canvassed the area and spotted a matching Dodge SUV leaving the neighborhood. Police attempted a traffic stop before the SUV could merge onto southbound I-5, but the driver refused to pull over.
Officers were authorized to begin pursuit heading south on I-5, though police eventually were forced to terminate the chase near the city limits, SPD said.

SPD said the Tacoma Police Department contacted the Dodge’s registered owner, who claimed the SUV had been stolen without having yet been reported. No arrests have been announced as the investigation continues.

The incident comes as Mayor Katie Wilson has signed off on the expansion of SPD’s Real Time Crime Center camera system that will include new installations on Capitol Hill in the Pike/Pine area and in the Central District around Garfield High School . Officials have vowed to address privacy and law enforcement overreach concerns identified in audits of the system.
Even as the the city moves forward with the new installations, SPD has access to Seattle Department of Transportation cameras in the area around where Saturday’s incident took place.

One audit found Real Time Crime Center staff have access to view 538 cameras under the current system. Private camera integrations through Axon’s “Connect Seattle” program also tie into the system, operating without caps, deployment criteria, or technical masking to prevent private areas such as residential windows from being filmed

articles.title: Wilson, Zahilay make their pick for interim leader to oversee downsizing of King County Regional Homelessness Authority
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and King County Executive Girmay Zahilay have tapped Mark Ellerbrook to serve as interim CEO of the King County Regional Homelessness Authority.

The move follows the resignation of Kelly Kinnison earlier this month . Kinnison was hired in 2024 as the troubled organization’s fifth leader and was part of the effort to surface the financial issues that have the authority in a $16.7 million hole.

Wilson and Zahilay’s announcement says Ellerbrook brings nearly 20 years of city and county experience in housing and government administration, most recently serving as as part of Wilson’s leadership team at City Hall. He will take a leave of absence from the city to step into the role.

With approval by the KCRHA Governing Board, the announcement says Ellerbrook’s priorities will include strengthening the agency’s financial controls, navigating uncertain federal Continuum of Care funding, and overseeing the January 1, 2027 transition of locally funded contracts back to Seattle and King County.
The downsizing of the authority began this summer as officials were forced to restructure the KCRHA after the audit was revealed.
The KCHRA’s budget was proposed as $205 million in 2026 with about 60% coming from Seattle and the rest from the county and state and federal pass-through grants.
Some continue to call for the downsizing organization to be shut down completely.

The authority was formed as officials pledged the new effort would consolidate efforts to address the homelessness crisis at a broader, more regional level. At one point growing to a $250 million a year effort, KCRHA was officially established in late 2019 through an Interlocal Agreement between the county and the City of Seattle under then- Mayor Jenny Durkan and then- King County Executive Dow Constantine .

articles.title: Seattle’s Best Late-Night Restaurants
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: Maybe it’s the wet and the gloom, maybe it’s the public transit system that slows to a crawl in the wee hours, or maybe it’s the fabled Seattle Freeze. Whatever the cause, our city’s late-night food scene is much-maligned, and there’s a grain of truth to this rep.

But if you know where to look, there are plenty of great places that stay open after 10 p.m., and even a handful after last call at 2 a.m. If there’s one thing we’ve learned in our relentless pursuit of a midnight (or much later) snack , it’s that the hours posted online are particularly unreliable for late-night spots. Instagram, a phone call, or word of mouth are typically your best bet for securing an after-hours bite. Well, that, and this list.
In our November 2026 update, we added Tacos Cometa, a Capitol Hill carne asada spot with fine dining pedigree, Jupiter Bar’s Good Shape Pizza, and reincarnated Seattle icon Bush Garden.
